templates.title: Order accuracy per merchant and week, with the merchant's own channel shown apart
templates.subtopic: DISTINCT before counting, LEFT JOIN of a flag onto every order, weekly buckets in a time zone

sections.scenario: A merchant's weekly report shows order accuracy: of the orders it delivered, how many came with an item missing or wrong. Consumers report problems after delivery, sometimes several times about one order, and they also report things that are not about the items at all (a late delivery, damaged packaging). Some merchants also take orders on their own website or app and use the marketplace only for delivery; those orders are reported on a separate row so a merchant can compare its two channels.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns merchant_id, week_start, channel, delivered_orders, inaccurate_orders, accuracy_rate, one row per merchant, week and channel with at least one delivered order, ordered by merchant_id, week_start, channel. Only orders with status = 'delivered' count; cancelled orders are in neither count. A delivered order is inaccurate if it has at least one report with issue_type missing_item or incorrect_item filed within {{window_h}} hours after delivered_at (reported_at <= delivered_at + {{window_h}} hours, this exercise's rule); other issue types do not count. An order with several qualifying reports is one inaccurate order. accuracy_rate is (delivered_orders − inaccurate_orders) / delivered_orders, rounded to 4 decimal places. A store belongs to the merchant in stores.merchant_id; a merchant's stores are added together. {{week_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). channel is marketplace or own_channel. The sample has {{orders}} orders and {{reports}} reports.
sections.assumptions: Merchants, stores, orders, reports and the report window are hypothetical; the window is this exercise's rule, so check current docs for how any real accuracy metric is defined. Reports carry no consumer identity, and the report is about the order, not about whoever delivered it.
sections.criteria: Cancelled orders excluded from both counts; only missing or incorrect item reports, inside the inclusive window (Hard+); one inaccurate order however many reports; delivered orders with no report kept through a LEFT JOIN; stores added up per merchant; channels shown apart; Monday weeks, in the store's local time at Very Hard; numeric division and correct rounding; deterministic order; sensible answers on disputes, small denominators and late reports.

clarifications.q: An order has a missing_item and an incorrect_item report. How many inaccurate orders is that?
clarifications.a: One. Accuracy is counted per order.

clarifications.q: A cancelled order has a missing_item report. Does it count anywhere?
clarifications.a: No. It was never delivered, so it is in neither the denominator nor the numerator.

clarifications.q: Is a report exactly {{window_h}} hours after delivery inside the window?
clarifications.a: Yes. The window is inclusive; one second later is outside.

clarifications.q: Does a delivered order with no report at all appear?
clarifications.a: Yes, in delivered_orders. Most orders have no report.

clarifications.q: How is accuracy_rate rounded?
clarifications.a: ROUND(…, 4) on a numeric, half away from zero.

hints: Build the set of inaccurate orders first: SELECT DISTINCT order_id from qualifying reports. That collapses repeated reports.
LEFT JOIN that set onto the delivered orders, so orders without a report stay in the denominator, and count the joined id.
Find the week with date_trunc('week', …), which starts weeks on Monday, after converting the timestamp to the time zone the report uses.
followups: Merchants dispute reports they think are wrong. How would you show accuracy both before and after disputes are resolved, without rewriting last month's published numbers?
A small merchant has 6 orders in a week and one problem, so its accuracy is 0.8333. How would you present a rate on so few orders honestly?
Reports arrive up to {{window_h}} hours after delivery. When is a week's number final, and how would you build the report incrementally until then?
Accuracy should be broken down by item, to tell a merchant which dishes go missing. What does the data need, and why does a report about one item not make the other items inaccurate?

rules.ask: An order has three reports. How many times does your query count it as inaccurate?
Where do the delivered orders with no report go in your query, and what happens to the denominator?
Where does a cancelled order with a report leave your query: before or after you count reports?
A store in Los Angeles delivers an order on Sunday evening local time. Which UTC week is that, and which week does the merchant expect to see it in?
Is the merchant's accuracy the average of its stores' rates, or the ratio of the totals? When do they differ?

templates.title: Membership value per month: fees waived against the monthly price, trial months shown apart
templates.subtopic: per member-month aggregation with a LEFT JOIN, conditional sums, strict thresholds, a ratio of members

sections.scenario: A delivery membership charges a monthly price and, under this exercise's rule, waives the delivery fee on orders above a minimum subtotal. The membership team wants to know, month by month, whether members get their money's worth: how much in delivery fees was waived, and what share of members saved more than they paid. Free trial months behave differently and are reported on their own row.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns month, plan_kind, members, waived_orders, fees_waived_cents, members_ahead, share_ahead, one row per month and plan kind ('paid' or 'trial', from is_trial) that has at least one member-month, ordered by month, plan_kind. A member-month is a row of member_months; an order belongs to the UTC calendar month of placed_at, and counts only if its consumer has a member-month for that month. A member's order has its delivery fee waived when it is delivered and meets the minimum subtotal; the amount waived is its delivery_fee_cents. {{min_rule}} Per member-month, add up the waived fees; the member is ahead when that total is strictly greater than its price_cents (for a trial month, the price it would have paid). members counts member-months, including those with no orders; waived_orders and fees_waived_cents add up the waived orders; members_ahead counts member-months that are ahead; share_ahead is members_ahead / members rounded to 4 decimal places.
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Amounts are integer cents. The sample has {{member_months}} member-months and {{orders}} orders.
sections.assumptions: The price, the minimum subtotal and the waiver are this exercise's rules with hypothetical numbers; check current docs for any real membership's terms. Orders by consumers who are not members that month are out of scope. The report is in aggregate; no consumer is shown individually.
sections.criteria: Only delivered orders in a member-month; the minimum inclusive and tested after promotions (Hard+), per vertical at Very Hard; fees summed per member-month before comparing; strict "ahead"; member-months without orders kept; trial months apart; correct rounding and order; good reasoning on annual plans, billing cycles and why waived fees are not cost.

clarifications.q: A member placed no orders this month. Are they in members?
clarifications.a: Yes. They paid (or trialled) and saved nothing; leaving them out would flatter the share.

clarifications.q: A member's waived fees equal the monthly price exactly. Are they ahead?
clarifications.a: No. Ahead means strictly greater.

clarifications.q: Is a subtotal exactly at the minimum enough?
clarifications.a: Yes. The minimum is inclusive.

clarifications.q: An order is placed at 23:59:59 UTC on the last day of a month by someone who joined the next month. Does it count?
clarifications.a: No. It belongs to the month of its placed_at, when they were not a member.

clarifications.q: Does a cancelled order waive anything?
clarifications.a: No. Only delivered orders count.

hints: Compute the waived orders first: delivered, in a member-month, meeting the minimum. Aggregate them per consumer and month.
LEFT JOIN that aggregate onto member_months, so every member-month is present, and treat a missing total as 0.
Then group by month and plan kind, with COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE waived > price_cents) for the members ahead.
followups: Members on an annual plan pay once a year. How would you compare their waived fees with a price, and what would you show for a member who cancelled in month three?
The share ahead rises in the month the minimum subtotal is lowered. How would you separate the effect of the rule change from a change in who joined?
Finance asks for the cost of the waiver. Why is fees_waived_cents not the cost, given that members order more often than they would without the membership?
Months must be the member's billing cycle (joined on the 17th, renews on the 17th), not calendar months. What changes in the data and the query?

rules.ask: A member placed no qualifying order this month. Is that member-month in your denominator?
A member's waived fees equal the price exactly. Are they ahead under the rule?
Which subtotal do you compare with the minimum: before or after the promotion?
An order at 23:59:59 on the 31st by someone who joined on the 1st of the next month. Where does it land?
Is the share of members ahead an average of something? What exactly is in the numerator and the denominator?

templates.title: Ordered while toggled off: items that were already marked unavailable
templates.subtopic: as-of join (latest row at or before a time), tie-breaks, scope precedence, two-level aggregation

sections.scenario: Convenience and grocery merchants mark items unavailable in their merchant tools when they run out, and back on when they restock. A consumer app that shows a stale menu can still take an order for an item the store had already switched off, which ends in a substitution or a refund. The catalogue team wants to measure, per store and day, how many orders contained an item that was switched off when the order was placed.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns store_id, order_date, orders, flagged_orders, flagged_lines, one row per store and UTC date of placed_at with at least one order, ordered by store_id, order_date. An order line's item was unavailable when the latest availability toggle for that item and store with toggled_at <= placed_at has is_available = false. Toggles after the order are ignored. If two toggles have the same toggled_at, the one with the higher toggle_id is the later one. An item with no toggle at or before the order is available. orders counts the store's orders that day, flagged_orders those with at least one unavailable line, and flagged_lines the unavailable lines. {{scope_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). An item appears at most once per order. The sample has {{orders}} orders and {{toggles}} toggles.
sections.assumptions: Stores, items and toggles are hypothetical. Nothing here says why an item was switched off or whether the order was later fulfilled; the measure is only "the item was off when the order was placed".
sections.criteria: The latest toggle at or before the order, with <= and the toggle_id tie-break (Hard+); later toggles ignored; no toggle means available; store scoping, and merchant-wide toggles with the latest of either scope winning (Very Hard); orders and lines counted separately; every store-day with orders present; deterministic order; credible answers on toggle delays and computing an as-of join at scale.

clarifications.q: The item was switched off at 10:00 and back on at 11:00, and the order was at 11:30. Is it flagged?
clarifications.a: No. Only the latest toggle at or before the order counts, and that one says available.

clarifications.q: A toggle and an order have exactly the same timestamp. Which comes first?
clarifications.a: The toggle applies: toggled_at <= placed_at.

clarifications.q: The item was switched off an hour after the order. Is the order flagged?
clarifications.a: No. Toggles after the order are ignored.

clarifications.q: The same item is switched off at another store. Does that matter?
clarifications.a: No. A store-level toggle applies to its own store only.

clarifications.q: An order has two unavailable lines. What do the columns show?
clarifications.a: One flagged order and two flagged lines.

hints: For every order line, find one toggle: the latest for that item and store at or before placed_at. A correlated subquery with ORDER BY toggled_at DESC, toggle_id DESC LIMIT 1, a LATERAL join, or DISTINCT ON all work.
Aggregate to one row per order (its count of unavailable lines) before aggregating to store and day, so flagged_orders counts orders, not lines.
Treat "no toggle found" (NULL) as available: compare with = false, not NOT …, or use COALESCE.
followups: Toggles arrive from merchants' tools with a delay of up to a few minutes. How would you report the orders that fall inside that uncertainty, rather than flagging them as if the timing were exact?
With billions of order lines and millions of toggles a day, the correlated lookup is too slow. How would you compute the as-of join in a warehouse, and what would you partition by?
The team wants "minutes the item had been off when the order arrived". What do you add, and how do you treat an item that was off since before your data starts?
Flagged orders lead to substitutions or refunds. How would you connect this measure to what actually happened to the line, without double-counting lines that were substituted and then refunded?

rules.ask: Your MAX finds the latest time. How do you get the is_available of that row, and what if two toggles share that time?
The item was switched off, then back on before the order. Does your EXISTS still flag it?
What is in your ORDER BY, and does it decide every tie?
Is flagged_orders counting orders or lines in your query? Show me with an order that has two unavailable items.
Your engine has an ASOF JOIN. How does it treat a toggle at exactly the order time, and is that what the rule says?

templates.title: Open stores at each order's time, from a week of opening hours
templates.subtopic: counting intervals containing a point with two bisects; intervals that wrap a cycle

sections.scenario: When a consumer orders, how much choice did they have? A city's analysts want, for every order in a period, the number of the city's stores that were open at that minute. Stores publish weekly opening hours: some open once a day, some close between lunch and dinner, and late-night stores stay open past midnight. There are thousands of stores and many more orders, so the count must be fast.
sections.problem: Implement open_store_counts(hours, orders). hours is a list of (store_id, day, open_min, close_min), one per opening interval: day is 0 (Monday) to 6 (Sunday) and the minutes count from that day's midnight, 0 <= open_min < 1440 and 0 <= close_min <= 1440, never equal. A store is open from open_min up to but not including close_min. A store's own intervals never overlap. orders is a list of integer minutes since Monday 00:00 of week 0. Return, for each order in input order, the number of stores open at that minute. {{midnight_rule}} {{weeks_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to about 3 000 stores (some 22 000 intervals) and 20 000 orders in the timing check. Checking every interval for every order is O(n·q) and too slow; so is scanning a start-sorted list until the starts pass the order, which is still O(n) per order. Something close to O((n + q) log n) is expected.
sections.assumptions: Stores and hours are hypothetical, and every time is in the city's local time with no daylight-saving change in the period. Holiday hours and temporary pauses are out of scope here. Because a store's intervals never overlap, counting open intervals counts open stores.
sections.criteria: Half-open intervals, open at the opening minute and closed at the closing minute; split lunch and dinner hours; at Hard+, intervals across midnight and the Sunday-to-Monday wrap split correctly, and a close of 0 or 1440 both meaning midnight; at Very Hard, orders reduced modulo the week and adjacent all-day intervals counted once at midnight; sorted starts and ends with two bisects per order (or a per-minute count array) rather than a scan; a clear complexity argument; sensible answers on holiday hours, pauses and streaming.

clarifications.q: A store opens at 11:00. Is an order at exactly 11:00 counted?
clarifications.a: Yes. An order at the closing minute is not.

clarifications.q: Do I need store ids at all?
clarifications.a: Not for the count, because a store's intervals never overlap. They matter for the follow-ups.

clarifications.q: Are the hours sorted?
clarifications.a: No. Intervals of different stores and days arrive in any order.

clarifications.q: Can I precompute an answer for every minute of the week?
clarifications.a: Yes, if you can explain the cost; the week has 10 080 minutes.

hints: Put every interval on one line of week minutes: it starts at day × 1440 + open_min.
A store is open at t if it started at or before t and has not yet ended. Count the starts <= t and subtract the ends <= t: two binary searches on two sorted lists.
An interval that runs past the end of the week wraps to Monday morning: split it into two pieces.
followups: Analysts want to know which stores were open, not just how many, for a sample of orders. What would you build, and what does it cost?
Stores publish holiday hours that replace the weekly hours on certain dates. How does your structure change?
Every store pauses itself now and then when the kitchen is busy, for minutes at a time. How would you include pauses without rebuilding everything for each one?
The orders arrive as a stream, all day. What would you keep in memory, and how would you handle a store that changes its hours during the week?

rules.ask: There are 22,000 intervals and 20,000 orders. How many comparisons is that, and how long in Python?
Why does starts-at-or-before minus ends-at-or-before give the number of open stores? When would it be wrong?
That precomputes the week. What happens to memory and build time if the analysts want seconds, or a year of holiday hours?
A store opens Sunday at 20:00 and closes at 03:00. Where does that interval go on your week line?
What does the tree give you here that two sorted lists do not?

templates.title: Repeat carts: orders that exactly repeat one of the same account's earlier carts
templates.subtopic: canonical form of a multiset (sorted tuple) as a dictionary key; most recent match per key

sections.scenario: Many orders are reorders: the same lunch every Tuesday, the same weekly shop. The consumer app wants to know how often a cart exactly repeats an earlier one, and which earlier order it repeats, to decide how prominently to offer "reorder". Carts are written in whatever order the consumer added items, sometimes with the same item on two lines, so two identical carts rarely look identical in the raw data. Workplace accounts that order for a whole office can have tens of thousands of orders.
sections.problem: Implement repeat_carts(orders). orders is a list of (order_id, account_id, lines) in the order they were placed. Two carts are the same when every line has the same total quantity in both. Return, for each order in input order, the order_id of the most recent earlier order by the same account with the same cart, or None if there is none. {{line_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 50 000 orders in the timing check, from two accounts with tens of thousands of orders each, carts of up to five lines. Comparing each order with every earlier one is O(k²·m) per account; keeping a list of earlier carts and testing cart in earlier is still O(k) per order and too slow. Something close to O(Σ m log m) is expected.
sections.assumptions: Accounts, items and orders are hypothetical. The analysis uses only the account id and the cart; prices, stores and delivery addresses are out of scope, and the result is used in aggregate.
sections.criteria: Line order ignored; quantities matter; only the same account; the most recent earlier match; subsets are not repeats; at Hard+, repeated items added up, zero lines ignored and empty carts returning None without ever matching; at Very Hard, options as part of the line, in any order, with an empty tuple equal to none; a canonical sorted tuple in a dictionary rather than a list scan; a clear complexity argument; good answers on near repeats, changing ids and incremental runs.

clarifications.q: Do the lines have to be in the same order?
clarifications.a: No. A cart is the set of lines with their quantities; the order the items were added does not matter.

clarifications.q: Is a cart that contains everything from an earlier one, plus one more item, a repeat?
clarifications.a: No. The carts must be exactly the same.

clarifications.q: Two earlier orders have the same cart. Which do I return?
clarifications.a: The most recent one before the current order.

clarifications.q: Does another account's identical cart count?
clarifications.a: No. Only the same account's earlier orders.

clarifications.q: Can I sort the lines and compare?
clarifications.a: Yes, that is the canonical form. The question is what you then do with it for 50 000 orders.

hints: Turn each cart into a canonical, hashable value: add up quantities per line key, drop zero quantities, and sort into a tuple.
Keep a dictionary from (account_id, canonical cart) to the most recent order_id. Look up before you store.
Each order then costs O(m log m) for its own lines and O(1) for the lookup, independent of how many orders came before.
followups: Product wants "near repeats": the same cart with one item more or less. How would you find them without comparing every pair of carts?
An item's id changes when the merchant rebuilds its menu, so last month's identical cart no longer matches. What would you key on instead, and what could go wrong?
The analysis runs daily over five years of orders. What state do you keep between runs, and how big is it?
How would you compute the same result in SQL over an order_lines table, and what plays the role of the canonical tuple there?

rules.ask: The office account has 25,000 orders. How many cart comparisons does cart in carts make over the whole run?
Does a set keep the quantities? What does your key say about two lattes against one?
Two lines of the same item with quantities 1 and 1. Does your sorted tuple equal the cart with one line of quantity 2?
You hash the cart into a short string. What happens on a collision, and do you need the hash at all when Python can key a dict on the tuple?
A Counter is not hashable. How do you turn it into a key, and what about zero counts?

templates.title: Substitutions that fill the most out-of-stock lines
templates.subtopic: augmenting paths with item capacities, greedy counterexamples

sections.scenario: A grocery order is being picked in a store, and some lines are out of stock. For each out-of-stock line, the consumer approved a short list of substitutes when they placed the order (or chose a refund instead). The store has a few units of each substitute on the shelf, and several lines often approve the same items: oat milk and soy milk may both be acceptable for two different milk lines. Before the shopper starts substituting, the picking app wants to know the most lines the shelf can cover, so it can tell the consumer how many lines will be refunded. Taking the first approved item for each line in turn is quick, but it can use up the only item another line would accept.
sections.problem: Implement most_lines_filled(orders). Each order is a dict with "lines", "units" and "reserved". "lines" is a list of (line_id, approved) pairs, one per out-of-stock line, where approved lists the item ids the consumer accepts as a substitute for that line (an empty list means the consumer chose a refund). "units" maps an item id to the units on the shelf. One unit fills one line, a line takes at most one unit, and a line can be filled only by an item on its own approved list. Return a list with, for each order in input order, the largest number of its lines that can be filled at the same time. {{level_rule}} Orders are independent: units never move from one order to another.
sections.constraints: Up to 2 000 orders per call, each with up to {{max_lines}} out-of-stock lines and up to 5 approved items per line. Trying every way to give units to lines is exponential in the number of lines, and taking the first approved item with a unit left is fast but returns too few lines. Something close to O(L · E) per order, for L lines and E approved pairs, is expected.
sections.assumptions: Items, shelves and orders are hypothetical. Substitution rules here are this exercise's rules; check current docs for how real substitution preferences work. Preference order inside an approved list does not matter for the count. Units on the shelf are exact (no phantom stock in this exercise).
sections.criteria: Item units used as capacities; repeated and unstocked approved items handled; empty approved lists never filled; (Very Hard) reserved units subtracted first and never below zero; independent orders; a correct augmenting-path or max-flow method with a clear argument for why greedy fails, illustrated by a small counterexample; a correct complexity statement.

clarifications.q: Does it matter which line gets which unit?
clarifications.a: Not for the answer, which is only the count. Any assignment that fills the most lines is fine.

clarifications.q: Can an item fill several lines?
clarifications.a: Yes, one line per unit. An item with three units can fill three lines.

clarifications.q: An approved item has no entry in "units".
clarifications.a: The store has none of it, so it fills nothing.

clarifications.q: Can a line take two units, say half from each of two items?
clarifications.a: No. A line is filled by exactly one unit of one approved item, or not at all.

clarifications.q: Is the consumer's first choice preferred?
clarifications.a: Not in this exercise. Follow-up 2 asks about it.

hints: Draw lines on one side and items on the other, with an edge for each approved pair. You want the largest set of edges where every line is used at most once and every item at most as many times as it has units.
When a line finds all its items full, ask whether one of the lines holding one of those items could move to another item it approves. That chain of moves is an augmenting path.
Give each item a list of the lines holding it. A depth-first search per line, with a visited set of items, finds an augmenting path or proves none exists for that line.
followups: Give an order where filling lines in order with each line's first available item fills fewer lines than possible, and one where "lines with the fewest options first" also fails.
The consumer ranks the approved items. Among all assignments that fill the most lines, you now want the one that uses first choices most often. What changes in the algorithm?

A substitute costs more than the original line, and the store absorbs at most a fixed amount of the difference per order (this exercise's rule). How does the problem change, and is it still a matching?
Shelf counts are uncertain: a unit the app thinks is there may not be. How would you present the count to the consumer, and what would you re-run when the shopper finds a shelf empty?

rules.ask: Two lines: one approves oat milk and soy milk, the other only oat milk, with one unit of each. What does your loop return, and what is the right answer?
Every line in this order approves exactly two items, so your sort changes nothing. Can a tie still lead the greedy to the wrong answer?
How many assignments does an order with {{max_lines}} lines and three approved items each have, and how many orders of that size does your code finish in a minute?
Why is it safe never to take a unit back once a line has been filled, and what bounds the total work per order?
Where do the item units go in your network, and how does the result differ from a matching where each item has one unit?

templates.title: Promotion price timeline — the price a consumer saw, segment by segment
templates.subtopic: min-heap with lazy deletion, tie-breaking, segment output

sections.scenario: Merchants and the marketplace run promotions on menu items: a lunch price on a bowl, a weekend price on a pizza, a flash deal for an hour. Promotions overlap, and when several apply at once, the consumer sees the lowest price. Support and merchant reporting both need to answer "what price did a consumer see for this item at 19:40 last Tuesday, and which promotion gave it?", and finance wants each item's history as a list of segments rather than a lookup per order. A merchant tool can create promotions in bulk, so a single item can have thousands of promotions active at once.
sections.problem: Implement price_timeline(base, promotions, horizon). Times are whole minutes from the start of the period, and the period is [0, horizon). base maps each item to its base price rows (time, price). {{base_rule}} promotions is a list of (promo_id, item, start, end, price) tuples, listed in the order they were created, oldest first; a promotion applies at minute t when start <= t < end. A promotion may start before 0 or end after horizon; only the part inside the period counts. At each minute, the winning promotion is the one with the lowest price among those that apply and whose price is strictly below the base price in force; on equal prices the older promotion wins. If no promotion wins, the consumer sees the base price and no promotion. Return a dict mapping every item in base to a list of (start, end, price, promo_id) segments that cover [0, horizon) in order, with promo_id set to None for the base price. A new segment starts exactly when the price or the winning promotion changes, so two adjacent segments never have both the same price and the same promotion. {{level_note}}
sections.constraints: Up to 100 000 promotions across all items, up to 50 000 on one item, and thousands active at the same minute. horizon is at most 525 600 (a year of minutes). Every promotion has start < end. Re-evaluating every active promotion at every boundary is too slow when thousands overlap; something close to O(n log n) is expected.
sections.assumptions: Items, prices and promotions are hypothetical, and how promotions combine is this exercise's rule (check current docs). Prices are integer cents. No two promotions share an id. Every promotion's item appears in base.
sections.criteria: Segments that cover the period exactly and change only when the price or the winning promotion changes; ties to the older promotion by creation order; promotions at or above the base never win; clipping at both ends; half-open ranges; (Very Hard) base price changes that make a promotion lose or win; a sweep with a heap and lazy deletion, or another O(n log n) structure, with a correct complexity statement and a clear reason why rescanning the active list fails at these sizes.

clarifications.q: What does "older" mean?
clarifications.a: Earlier in the promotions list. It is not the earlier start.

clarifications.q: Two promotions with the same price, but different ids, follow each other. One segment or two?
clarifications.a: Two. The winning promotion changed, so a new segment starts, even though the price is the same.

clarifications.q: A promotion is priced exactly at the base price.
clarifications.a: It never wins. The consumer sees the base price, with no promotion.

clarifications.q: Can a promotion end exactly when another starts?
clarifications.a: Yes. Ranges are half-open, so at the shared minute only the second applies.

clarifications.q: Is the output per minute?
clarifications.a: No. Segments only; the period can be a year of minutes.

hints: The winner can only change at a promotion's start, at a promotion's end or at a base price change. Visit those times in order.
Keep the active promotions in a min-heap keyed by (price, creation index). The top is the winner, if it is still active and below the base price.
You do not need to remove a promotion from the middle of the heap when it ends. Store its end with it, and pop the top while the top has already ended.
followups: Support asks for the price at one minute for millions of orders. Once the segments exist, how do you answer each lookup?
Some promotions are a percentage off rather than a fixed price. What changes when the base price changes during a promotion?
A promotion is cancelled after it ran, and finance wants the timeline as it was shown, and as it would be now. How do you keep both?
The timeline must be kept up to date as promotions are created all day. What do you recompute when one promotion is added?

rules.ask: How many boundaries and how many active promotions does the largest item have, and how many comparisons does your loop make?
Removing from the middle of a list is O(a). With thousands active, what does your sweep cost in total, and what would you keep instead?
Your heap still holds promotions that have ended. Why is it enough to look only at the top, and how large can the heap grow?
After sorting, how do you still know which of two equal-priced promotions is older?
Your sorted list keeps comparisons logarithmic, but what does each insert and delete move in memory, and when would that matter?

templates.title: Debug the cart total calculator
templates.subtopic: modifiers, promotion order, membership minimum, tax base, rounding once

sections.scenario: The checkout page shows a cart total before the consumer places an order. Support has passed on several complaints. Two burgers with extra cheese were charged the cheese once. A consumer with an item on promotion and a 20%-off order code got more off than the code allows. A member was charged a delivery fee on an order whose items were above the membership minimum, after a code brought the total below it. Tax looks too high on discounted orders. Totals on carts with several discounted items are a cent out. The calculator below is the suspect.
sections.problem:
Fix price_carts(carts, fees) so that it meets this specification (this exercise's rules; check current docs for real fee, membership and tax rules). {{replay_rule}}

  1. fees is {"delivery", "member_min", "tax_bps"}: the delivery fee in cents, the membership minimum subtotal in cents, and the tax rate in basis points (800 is 8%).
  2. Lines. Each cart is {"member", "lines", "order_promo"}. Each line is {"item", "price", "qty", "modifiers", "promo_pct"}. Modifier prices are per unit, so a line's total is (price + sum of its modifier prices) × qty. The subtotal is the sum of line totals.
  3. Promotions. An item-level promotion takes promo_pct per cent off its line's total. Item-level promotions apply first. order_promo is None or {"pct", "max_off"}: pct per cent off the subtotal after item-level promotions, but never more than max_off cents.
  4. Rounding. The discounted subtotal (subtotal minus every discount) is computed exactly and rounded once to whole cents, halves rounded up. discount is the subtotal minus the discounted subtotal.
  5. Membership. The delivery fee is waived for a member whose subtotal before any promotion is at least member_min.
  6. Tax is tax_bps basis points of the discounted subtotal, rounded to whole cents, halves rounded up. The delivery fee is not taxed in this exercise.
  7. Output. One dict per cart, in order: {"subtotal", "discount", "delivery_fee", "tax", "total"}, all integer cents, with total = discounted subtotal + delivery_fee + tax.
sections.constraints: Keep the function's name, arguments and output format. Amounts stay exact: no floats. Up to 100 000 carts per call, processed in linear time.
sections.assumptions: Prices, fees, tax rates, promotions and the membership minimum are hypothetical. Service fees, tips and small-order fees are out of scope. No discount takes a line below zero, since every percentage is at most 100.
sections.criteria: Finds and explains every bug with its consumer-facing symptom; modifiers per unit; item promotions before the order promotion and its cap; the membership minimum on the subtotal before promotions; tax on the discounted subtotal; one exact rounding, halves up; integer cents throughout; minimal fixes, with a test per bug.

clarifications.q: Is the membership minimum tested before or after promotions?
clarifications.a: Before, in this exercise: on what the consumer put in the cart.

clarifications.q: Which subtotal is taxed?
clarifications.a: The discounted one, after it has been rounded to cents.

clarifications.q: Why round only once?
clarifications.a: Rounding each line's discount separately can move the total by a cent per line, and the consumer sees a different number on the receipt.

clarifications.q: Is round() fine for halves?
clarifications.a: Python's round() rounds halves to even, so 904.5 becomes 904. The rule here is halves up.

clarifications.q: How many bugs are there?
clarifications.a: Several, of different kinds. Each check points at one.

hints: Work out by hand: two cheeseburgers at 850 with a 150 modifier. What is the line total?
Which amount is the order promotion taken from, and which amount decides the membership waiver?
Find every place an amount is rounded. How many should there be before the discounted subtotal?
followups: The order promotion also has a minimum subtotal to qualify. Which subtotal should it test, and what do consumers see if it differs from the membership rule?
A refund is issued for one line after delivery. How do you split the order discount and the tax back to that line so that refunds of every line add up to what was charged?
Tax rates differ by item type (prepared food versus groceries) in some places. What changes in the calculation and in the output?
The checkout total and the total charged must match exactly, but they are computed by two services. How do you keep them from drifting?

rules.ask: What does your code return for a discounted subtotal of exactly 904.5 cents, and does it match the rule "halves up"?
Where exactly does your one rounding happen, and what happens to the precision of a 33% discount before it?
If you round each line's discount, how far can a ten-line cart drift from rounding once, and in which direction?
A consumer adds a promotion code and loses free delivery. Under this exercise's rule, should that happen, and how would you test it?
Which amount does your tax use, and what would a tax authority expect when the discount is funded by the merchant?

templates.title: Menu ingestion from merchants' point-of-sale integrations
templates.subtopic: full and partial menu updates, validation, versioned publishing, freshness

sections.scenario: About {{stores}} stores sell through a delivery marketplace, and many of them connect their own point-of-sale system so that their menu stays in one place. The marketplace integrates with {{pos_kinds}} kinds of point-of-sale systems, each with its own format. Some send the whole menu, up to {{max_items}} items with categories, modifier groups and prices; others send partial updates such as one item's price or "this item is sold out". Merchants expect a price change or a sold-out item to show to consumers within {{freshness}}. A menu that arrives broken must never replace a good one, and consumers must never see an item that the store cannot make.
sections.problem: Design the pipeline that ingests menus from point-of-sale integrations and publishes them to consumers. Cover the canonical menu model you map every format to; how full menus and partial updates are applied; how availability updates take a faster path than full menus; validation and what happens to a menu that fails it; how a published menu is versioned and rolled back; how you meet the freshness target; and what you measure per integration and per store.
sections.constraints: Updates can arrive out of order and more than once. A full menu can be sent every few minutes even when nothing changed. Some systems use their own item ids that change when a merchant rebuilds a menu. Store hours and menu hours come in the same feeds. A merchant sees only its own stores' menus and errors.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, formats and targets are hypothetical; nothing here describes a real integration. You may use common building blocks: an API gateway, a queue or log, object storage, a relational or document store, a cache and a search index.
sections.criteria: A canonical menu model; full and partial updates with ordering and dedup; a fast path for availability and prices; validation with quarantine and a kept last-good version; atomic, versioned publishing with rollback; hashing to absorb unchanged resends; stable item identity across rebuilds; per-integration and per-store freshness and error metrics; merchant-scoped visibility; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: Who owns the menu when a merchant edits it in the marketplace tools too?
clarifications.a: You decide and explain it per field; the merchant must be able to see which source won.

clarifications.q: What makes a menu invalid?
clarifications.a: Your call: for example, prices of zero, modifier groups whose minimum exceeds their options, items in no category, or a menu that dropped 90% of its items at once.

clarifications.q: Must a sold-out item disappear, or show as unavailable?
clarifications.a: Either, but it must not be orderable within {{freshness}}.

clarifications.q: Can a full menu be applied partially?
clarifications.a: You decide. Say what a consumer sees while it is being applied.

hints: Separate structure (items, categories, modifiers), prices and availability: they change at very different rates and have different freshness needs.
Hash each normalised full menu so that an unchanged resend costs almost nothing.
Publish whole menu versions atomically, and keep the previous good version to fall back to.
followups: A point-of-sale system resends the whole menu every two minutes for every store. How do you keep that from flooding the pipeline and the search index?
A merchant rebuilds their menu and every item id changes. How do you keep order history, ratings and item-level reporting linked?
A full menu arrives that removes 1,800 of 2,000 items. Publish, hold, or ask the merchant, and on what evidence?
A sold-out update arrives before the full menu that contains the item. What does your pipeline do with it?
Analysts want "the menu as consumers saw it at 18:30 last Friday" for any store. What do you keep to answer it?

rules.ask: A sold-out flag arrives, then a full menu sent five minutes earlier is processed after it. Which state does the store end up in under your rule?
What exactly do you hash, and how do you stop a reordered but unchanged menu from looking new?
An integration's webhooks stop for an hour without errors. How do you notice, and what do consumers see meanwhile?
A price changed but consumers keep seeing the old one for twenty minutes. Where is it cached, and how is it invalidated within {{freshness}}?
A menu fails validation at 11:55, just before lunch. What does the merchant see, and what do consumers keep seeing?

incidents: One point-of-sale kind starts sending prices in dollars instead of cents after an update; 3% of stores show items at a hundredth of their price for {{freshness}} before anyone notices.
A merchant's system resends a full menu with every modifier group missing; the pipeline publishes it, and consumers order burgers with no way to choose a side.

templates.title: White-label delivery for merchants' own ordering channels
templates.subtopic: quotes, acceptance, status webhooks, per-channel reporting

sections.scenario: Merchants with their own website or app take orders themselves and use a delivery service, described here generally, to deliver them: their site asks for a delivery quote, shows the fee and estimated time to the consumer, and accepts the quote when the consumer pays. About {{merchants}} merchants send about {{daily_requests}} delivery requests a day. A quote is valid for {{quote_ttl}} (this exercise's rule). After acceptance, the merchant's site receives status updates (accepted, courier assigned, picked up, delivered, cancelled) to show its own consumers. Merchants want reports per ordering channel: their website, their app and their phone orders. Assigning couriers is out of scope: a service you are given does it and emits status events.
sections.problem: Design the merchant-facing API and the data flow behind it. Cover quote requests and their expiry; acceptance that is safe to retry; how status updates reach merchants reliably and in a useful order; what the merchant can query when it misses an update; cancellations from either side and what is charged; the per-channel reporting merchants see; and the data each merchant can and cannot see.
sections.constraints: Merchants' servers time out and retry; a quote may be accepted twice. Merchants' webhook endpoints are sometimes down for hours. Status events from the delivery service can arrive out of order. Courier information shown to a merchant is limited to what the delivery needs (for example a first name and a live status), never ratings or history; reports show couriers only in aggregate. A merchant sees only its own deliveries.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, fees, quote windows and cancellation rules are hypothetical; check current docs for any real product's rules. You may use common building blocks: an API gateway, a relational store, a log or queue, a webhook sender and a warehouse.
sections.criteria: Quotes as stored, expiring objects; idempotent acceptance; a delivery state machine with ranked, versioned updates; reliable webhooks through an outbox with retries, plus a query endpoint as the source of truth; clear cancellation and charge rules; per-channel reports at a stated grain; strict per-merchant visibility and minimal courier data, aggregate only in reports; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: Can the fee change between quote and acceptance?
clarifications.a: Not within {{quote_ttl}}; after that the quote is expired and the merchant must ask again.

clarifications.q: What identifies a delivery?
clarifications.a: The merchant's own order reference plus a delivery id you issue. You decide which one makes acceptance safe to retry.

clarifications.q: Must webhooks arrive in order?
clarifications.a: The merchant wants a sensible final state. Say what you guarantee.

clarifications.q: How does a merchant tag the channel?
clarifications.a: A field on the quote request; reports group by it.

hints: Make the quote a stored object with its own id and expiry, and make acceptance refer to it, with an idempotency key from the merchant.
Give every delivery state a rank and a version, so a merchant can ignore an older update that arrives late.
Keep an outbox of webhook deliveries with retries and backoff, plus a "get delivery" endpoint as the source of truth.
followups: A merchant's server accepts the same quote twice within a second because of a timeout. Walk through what happens.
The merchant's webhook endpoint is down for six hours. What happens to the updates, and what does the merchant see when it recovers?
A delivery is cancelled after the courier picked up the food. Which events, charges and report rows does that produce under your design?
A merchant wants delivery times per channel compared with their own in-store pickup times. What can you report, and what data must not leave your side?
At {{daily_requests}} requests a day, most quotes are never accepted. How long do you keep them, and what do they tell the merchant?

rules.ask: The key is reused with a different quote id. What do you return, and why?
A merchant's endpoint returns 200 but drops the update. How do they recover, and how do you know it happened?
Status events for one delivery arrive delivered-then-picked-up. What does the merchant's webhook stream show, and what does your state table hold?
Which courier fields does the merchant receive, for how long, and which never appear in reports?
A consumer pays at {{quote_ttl}} plus three seconds. What does the merchant's acceptance return, and what does the consumer see?

incidents: A merchant's retry bug accepts every quote twice for a day; without idempotency, 4% of their orders get two deliveries.
The webhook sender falls six hours behind after a deploy; merchants show "preparing" for orders already delivered, and support contacts spike.

templates.title: Menus as data — categories, items, modifier groups with minimum and maximum selections, prices per channel, menu hours, and the menu as it stood on a date
templates.subtopic: menu trees with shared and nested modifier groups, selection rules, channel prices, versioning, order lines frozen at order time

channel_list: the marketplace app and the merchant's own ordering site
the marketplace app, pickup orders and the merchant's own ordering site

sections.scenario: Restaurants list their menus on a local commerce marketplace: about {{stores}} store locations, with a typical menu of about {{items_per_menu}} items, and about {{menu_changes}} menu changes a day arriving from merchant tools and point-of-sale integrations. A menu has categories and items. Items have modifier groups such as "Choose a size" or "Add toppings", each with a minimum and a maximum number of selections, and an option can carry its own nested group (a combo's drink choice, then that drink's size). Many items share one group: a "Choose a sauce" group can sit on forty items. In this exercise one item can carry a different price on each channel ({{channel_list}}), and menus have hours: a breakfast menu until 11:00, a late-night menu after 22:00 (this exercise's rules; check current docs). Consumers, merchants and support all ask the same question in different words: what was on the menu, at what price, when this order was placed?
sections.problem: Design the data model for menus. Cover menus and their hours; categories; items; modifier groups and options, including shared groups and nested groups; prices per channel and per menu; and the link from an order line to the exact item, options and prices the consumer chose. Show how you answer "the menu as it stood at store S on channel C at time T", how you validate a cart line against the minimum and maximum selection rules, and how a merchant's change is recorded so that nothing a consumer saw is lost.
sections.constraints: Money is stored in integer cents. A shared modifier group is one object: changing it changes every item that uses it from that moment, and never retroactively. Nested groups go at most three levels deep in this exercise. Nothing is overwritten: an order placed yesterday must still show the names, options and prices the consumer chose, even after an item is renamed or deleted. Item ids from a merchant's point-of-sale can change when the merchant re-syncs a whole menu (this exercise's model). Menu hours are in the store's local time.
sections.assumptions: Store counts, menu sizes, change volumes and channels are hypothetical. Whether an item is in stock is a single flag here (availability is a Loop 4 topic). Tax, promotions and dish search are out of scope.
sections.criteria: A menu tree with shared and nested modifier groups and their selection rules; versioning chosen and costed (node-level effective dating or immutable published versions); channel and menu prices with a stated precedence; menu hours in local time; order lines frozen against immutable versions with the prices applied; stable item identity across point-of-sale re-syncs; cart validation written correctly for nested required groups; incidents explained and repaired without rewriting history.

clarifications.q: Is the price on the item or on the menu?
clarifications.a: Your choice. In this exercise one item can sit on a lunch menu and a dinner menu at different prices, so say where that difference lives.

clarifications.q: Can an option change the price?
clarifications.a: Yes, by a delta ("Large" adds 150 cents); a nested option can add its own delta on top.

clarifications.q: Does a full menu sync from the point-of-sale replace everything?
clarifications.a: It sends the whole menu. Items that did not change must keep their identity, so sales history and ratings stay continuous.

clarifications.q: Two menus are open at 10:30 and both list the same item at different prices. What does the consumer see?
clarifications.a: The item once. In this exercise the price of the menu that opened later wins; say where that rule is recorded.

clarifications.q: Does a required group stay required when its parent option is not chosen?
clarifications.a: No. A nested group applies only when its parent option is selected.

hints: Separate the structure (menu → category → item → modifier group → option → nested group) from the versions of each node. A shared group is one node that many items reference.
Choose between effective-dated rows per node and an immutable published version of the whole menu per change, and cost both at {{menu_changes}} changes a day.
The order line should point at immutable versions (or carry a frozen copy) of the item and of every option chosen, with the prices applied.
followups: Write the validation of a cart line against its modifier groups: minimum and maximum selections, and a nested group that is required only when its parent option is chosen.
A shared "Choose a sauce" group gains an option with a price. Which rows change, and what does an order placed an hour earlier show on its receipt?
A merchant re-syncs from its point-of-sale and every item id changes. How do you keep item history continuous for sales reports?
Compare a full published-menu snapshot per change with per-node effective-dated rows at {{stores}} stores and {{menu_changes}} changes a day. Estimate storage and the cost of "the menu as of T".
The same item is on the breakfast menu and the all-day menu at different prices, both open at 10:30, on {{channel_list}}. Which price does each channel show, and where is that decided?

rules.ask: With the whole menu stored as one document per store, how do you answer "which items used the sauce group last month" and "the price of item X on channel C at T" without reading every version?
A price changed at 14:00 and an order from 13:55 is refunded at 15:00. Which price does the refund use, and where does your model keep it?
How do you read one item with all its nested groups in a single query, and what stops a group from containing itself?
A merchant changes one price. How many rows does a new snapshot write at {{items_per_menu}} items, and how do you diff two versions for the merchant's change log?
The point-of-sale re-issues every item id after a re-sync. What is your stable key, and how do you match the new ids to the old items?

incidents: After a large chain re-synced its menus from its point-of-sale, every item looked new: item-level sales history and ratings reset in all its stores, because the item key was the point-of-sale id.

A shared modifier group was edited to remove an option. Receipts for the previous week lost that option's name, and the refund tool computed lower refunds, because order lines referenced the live group rather than a version.
With {{menu_changes}} changes a day, a job that rebuilt each store's whole published menu for every change fell behind at lunchtime, and consumers saw prices up to 20 minutes old.

templates.title: Store hours as data — weekly hours across midnight, holiday hours, temporary pauses, local time zones, and whether a store was open at a given moment
templates.subtopic: schedule versions, date overrides, pauses, wall-clock rules versus UTC instants, daylight-saving transitions, derived open intervals

sections.scenario: About {{stores}} restaurants and stores across {{time_zones}} time zones list their hours on a local commerce marketplace. Regular weekly hours can be split into lunch and dinner, and late-night stores close after midnight. Merchants add holiday hours for particular dates, and pause a store temporarily from a tablet or portal when the kitchen is overwhelmed, with or without a planned end; in this exercise the system also pauses a store when its order tablet stops responding. There are about {{pauses_per_day}} pauses a day. The consumer app asks "is this store open now, and when does it next open?" about {{open_checks}} times a second; scheduled orders ask the same about a future moment; support and merchant reports ask whether a store was open at a moment in the past.
sections.problem: Design the data model for store hours. Cover weekly hours with intervals that cross midnight; holiday hours for a date; temporary pauses, planned or open-ended, with who or what started and ended them; each store's time zone; daylight-saving transitions; and history, so that "was store S open at instant T" has the same answer today as it would have had then. Define precisely the rule that resolves weekly hours, holiday hours and pauses into open or closed at an instant, and design the derived structure that serves "open now" and "next open" at scale.
sections.constraints: Hours are stated in the store's local wall-clock time; instants are stored in UTC. A merchant's edit applies from the moment it is saved and never changes the past. In this exercise a date's holiday hours replace that date's weekly hours, and an interval that opens before midnight belongs to the date it opens on, so a holiday never shortens the previous night's late shift. On a night when the clocks change, a store listed 22:00 to 02:00 is open for 3 or 5 hours of elapsed time, not 4 (this exercise's rule: wall-clock hours are honoured). Pauses carry no individual staff identifiers in analytics.
sections.assumptions: Store counts, time zones, pause volumes and request rates are hypothetical. Menu hours (DSH-L3-01) and item availability are out of scope. Hours and pause behaviour are this exercise's model; check current docs for how real merchant tools work.
sections.criteria: Weekly schedule versions, date overrides and pauses kept apart, with a precise resolution rule and its reason codes; intervals across midnight belonging to the date they open; wall-clock hours converted to UTC with time zone rules, never fixed offsets; history reproducible for past instants; a derived interval table sized and refreshed on edit, pause and daylight-saving change; pause source and open-ended pauses modelled; incidents explained and corrected.

clarifications.q: Does a holiday entry affect the previous night's late shift?
clarifications.a: No. In this exercise hours belong to the date they open on.

clarifications.q: How is "open 24 hours" written?
clarifications.a: Your choice; say how you keep it apart from an interval whose open and close times are equal by mistake.

clarifications.q: Can a store's time zone change?
clarifications.a: Rarely, and usually as a data correction. Say whether past answers move when it is corrected.

clarifications.q: What should "next open" return during a pause with no planned end?
clarifications.a: Unknown. The app shows "temporarily closed"; model that state explicitly.

clarifications.q: Who can end an automatic pause?
clarifications.a: In this exercise the system ends it when the tablet responds again, unless the merchant has paused the store as well.

hints: Keep three sources apart: versions of the weekly schedule, date overrides, and pauses. Derive open intervals in UTC from them; never store only a computed flag.
Version the schedule itself (valid from, valid to) so a past instant is answered with the schedule in force then.
Materialise each store's open intervals in UTC for the next few weeks, recomputed on every edit and across daylight-saving changes; "open now" becomes an interval lookup minus active pauses.
followups: Write the resolution as pseudocode: input (store, instant); output open or closed and the reason (weekly hours, holiday hours, paused, outside hours).
A store listed 22:00 to 02:00 on the night the clocks go forward, and on the night they go back. What UTC intervals do you store each night?
A merchant edits Saturday's hours on Friday evening. Which derived rows change, and what does "was it open last Saturday at 23:00" return afterwards?
At {{open_checks}} checks a second across {{stores}} stores, where does the derived interval table live, and how quickly must a new pause reach it?
Scheduled orders were placed a week ahead for a date the store later marks as closed for a holiday. Which tables tell you, and what should happen to those orders?

rules.ask: A store lists 22:00 to 02:00 local. On the night the clocks go back, what UTC interval do you store, and how long is the store open?
A boolean "open now" is refreshed by a job. How do you answer whether the store was open last Tuesday at 21:30, and what happens when the job runs late?
Tuesday's hours are 17:00 to 01:30, and Wednesday is a holiday with the store closed all day. Is it open at 00:45 on Wednesday in your model?
A merchant pauses the store. How quickly must every cached "open now" answer change, and what invalidates it?
You stored an offset per store. What happens to a late-night store's intervals on the night the clocks change?

incidents: On the night the clocks went back, late-night stores across {{time_zones}} time zones showed as closed for their last hour: open intervals had been computed from local times with a fixed UTC offset per store.
A batch of holiday hours was saved as changes to the weekly schedule instead of date overrides, so the change applied to every following week, and hundreds of stores showed as closed every Thursday.

During a network outage, automatic pauses fired for thousands of stores. With {{pauses_per_day}} pauses a day normally, the spike was not noticed, and many stores stayed closed for an hour after their tablets reconnected because the automatic pauses had been recorded as merchant pauses with no end.

templates.title: Convenience and grocery catalogue as data — master items, store listings, availability signals, substitution preferences per line, and what was found, substituted or refunded
templates.subtopic: master catalogue and store listings, item matching with confidence and corrections, signals as events, preferences frozen on the line, outcomes that reconcile

sections.scenario: A local commerce marketplace sells from {{stores}} convenience and grocery stores. Each merchant sends its catalogue as feeds, with its own item ids, names, sizes and prices, about {{feed_updates}} updates a day. The marketplace keeps one master catalogue of about {{master_items}} products, identified by barcode where one exists, and about {{listings}} store listings link a store's item to a master item. Availability evidence arrives from merchant feeds, from shoppers' pick outcomes (found or not found) and from recent sales. When ordering, the consumer sets a substitution preference per line: a specific replacement they chose, "best match", or "refund if unavailable" (this exercise's choices; check current docs). After the order, each line ends found, substituted (with what), or refunded (for how much), possibly in part.
sections.problem: Design the data model for the catalogue and its order outcomes. Cover master items and product families (a single can and a 6-pack); store listings and their versions; the mapping from a merchant's item to a master item, including uncertain matches and corrections; availability signals per listing over time; the substitution preference captured on the order line; and per-line outcomes with quantities and amounts. Show the queries for: the found rate per master item, region and week; which substitutes were given for a master item and how often the consumer had named them; and, for one order, what the consumer asked for and what they received.
sections.constraints: Money is stored in integer cents. Sold-by-weight items are ordered as an estimate and charged by the picked weight (this exercise's rule). Merchant feeds rename items, change barcodes, and sometimes reuse an item id for a different product. Listings and mappings are effective-dated and never overwritten. The quantities on a line's outcomes must add up to the ordered quantity. Consumer data appears in analytics only in aggregate; the order's own record is visible to that consumer and to support. A merchant sees only its own stores.
sections.assumptions: Store counts, catalogue size, listing count and feed volume are hypothetical. Deciding the availability state shown to consumers is a Loop 4 topic; here you model the evidence. The "best match" ranking is a function you are given.
sections.criteria: Master items, product families, versioned listings and an explicit mapping with source, confidence and correction history; signals as append-only events; preferences and listing versions frozen on the order line; outcome rows that reconcile to the ordered quantity, with weighted items handled; precise found-rate definitions; incremental listing versions sized against volume; consumer data aggregated and merchants scoped to their stores; incidents explained and repaired by restating from stored history.

clarifications.q: Is a barcode unique?
clarifications.a: Mostly. Produce and deli use store-generated codes, and a manufacturer can reuse a barcode for a new product years later.

clarifications.q: What does "best match" record?
clarifications.a: The ranked candidates returned by the function you are given, its version, and which candidate was used.

clarifications.q: Partial fulfilment?
clarifications.a: Of 4 units, 3 can be found and 1 substituted or refunded according to the preference. The outcome rows must reconcile to 4.

clarifications.q: Can a merchant item map to two master items?
clarifications.a: Not at the same time. A wrong mapping is corrected, and history keeps both the wrong one and the correction.

clarifications.q: The consumer's named replacement is also unavailable.
clarifications.a: In this exercise the line is refunded; record that the named replacement was tried.

hints: Three layers: the master item (product identity), the listing (store × merchant item, versioned), and the mapping between them with its source (barcode, manual review, a model's match) and confidence.
Availability signals are append-only events per listing with an observed time and a source; never a single mutable flag.
The order line freezes the listing version and the preference; outcomes are rows (found, substituted, refunded) with quantities and amounts.
followups: A merchant reuses item id 4411 for a different product. What happens to its listings, mappings and last month's found rate for the old product?
Define the found rate for a master item per region and week precisely. What is the denominator when a line was found in part?
Two stores of one merchant describe the same product as "12 oz" and "355 ml". How does your matching normalise units, and when does a person review a match?
With {{listings}} listings and {{feed_updates}} feed updates a day, how do you store listing versions without rewriting rows that did not change?
A wrong mapping is discovered after a month. Which reports change when you correct it, and how do you restate them?

rules.ask: A manufacturer reuses a barcode for a new product, and produce uses store codes. What is your master key, and what role does the barcode play?
A feed says in stock at 09:00 and a pick says not found at 09:20. What does your model store, and how would a later reader see both?
If the substitute replaces the ordered item on the line, how do you report what the consumer asked for, and the found rate of the original item?
Ordered as "about 4 bananas", picked as 0.83 kg. What is stored, what is charged, and which quantity does the found rate use?
A match was wrong for a month before anyone noticed. Which rows does the correction write, and which historical numbers move?

incidents: One merchant's feed put sizes in the name field for a day. The matcher created thousands of new master items, and the found rates of the real products dropped because their listings had been remapped.
The found rate for produce in one region halved overnight: pick outcomes for sold-by-weight items were recorded as not found whenever the picked weight was below the estimate.
With {{listings}} listings, a nightly job that wrote a new version of every listing whether it had changed or not doubled storage each month, and "listing as of a date" queries scanned every version.

templates.title: Membership as data — plans, trials, monthly and annual billing, pauses and cancellations, and the benefit applied to each order
templates.subtopic: memberships and their periods, plan versions, billing attempts, grace, benefit decisions per order with reproducible inputs, revenue spread over months

sections.scenario: A local commerce marketplace sells a membership with monthly and annual plans. In this exercise members get a $0 delivery fee and a reduced service fee on orders from eligible stores whose subtotal is at least {{min_subtotal}} (this exercise's rule; check current docs). There are about {{members}} members, the monthly price is {{monthly_price}} (hypothetical), and new members can start with a free trial of {{trial_days}} days. Members can pause, cancel (effective at the end of the paid period), switch between monthly and annual, or have a renewal payment fail and enter a grace period while it is retried. Every order must record whether a membership benefit applied, which membership period it came from, and what it saved the consumer. Finance, product and support ask how many members are active, what memberships earn and cost, and why an order did or did not get the benefit.
sections.problem: Design the data model for the membership. Cover plans and plan versions (price changes); memberships and their periods (trial, paid, grace, paused); billing attempts and charges; cancellations, switches and refunds (this exercise's rules); and the benefit decision per order, with its inputs and the fees it waived. Show the queries for: members on a date by state; benefit cost and revenue per member-month, with annual plans spread across months; and "why didn't order O get free delivery".
sections.constraints: Money is stored in integer cents. A membership's periods never overlap. A price change applies from a member's next renewal (this exercise's rule). The benefit decision must be reproducible from stored inputs: in this exercise the subtotal is measured on items before promotions and before fees. Benefits continue during the grace period and after a cancellation until the paid period ends (this exercise's rules). Analytics see members in aggregate; support sees one member's own record.
sections.assumptions: Member counts, prices, the minimum subtotal and the trial length are hypothetical. Payment processing itself, and how a store becomes eligible, are out of scope; eligibility is an input recorded at order time.
sections.criteria: Plans with versions; memberships with non-overlapping periods carrying state and plan version; billing attempts, charges and refunds as money records; this exercise's rules for trials, grace, cancellation and price changes applied by period; one benefit decision of record per order with reproducible inputs; annual revenue spread across months; members-by-state on a date answered from periods; aggregates for analytics and member-scoped support views; incidents explained and repaired by correcting periods and decisions, not by editing totals.

clarifications.q: Is the trial a period with price 0?
clarifications.a: Yes, in this exercise. It converts to a paid period at its end unless the member cancels first.

clarifications.q: What happens when a renewal payment fails?
clarifications.a: A grace period of a few days while retries run; benefits continue during grace in this exercise, and the membership ends if every retry fails.

clarifications.q: Is there a refund on cancellation?
clarifications.a: In this exercise, only if no benefit was used in the current period; otherwise benefits continue to the period's end with no refund.

clarifications.q: How does an annual plan appear in monthly reports?
clarifications.a: Its charge is spread evenly across the twelve months it covers; a refund reverses the months not yet used.

clarifications.q: An order is edited after it was placed.
clarifications.a: The benefit is decided again on the edited order; say how you keep one decision of record per order.

hints: Separate the membership (the relationship), its periods (time slices with a state and a plan version) and the money (charges, refunds). Never rely on a single status column.
A benefit decision per order stores its inputs (subtotal, store eligibility, the membership period in force) and its outputs (fees waived), so it can be reproduced.
Store period boundaries as UTC instants, and decide which time zone defines a member's "day" for trials and renewals.
followups: Write the query for members on a date by state: trial, paid, grace, paused.
A member switches from monthly to annual halfway through a month. Which rows are written, and how is the unused half month handled in this exercise?
The price rises from {{monthly_price}} for new periods from next month. What changes for an existing member at renewal, and how does monthly revenue report it?
Support asks why order O did not get free delivery. Produce the evidence from your tables.
At {{members}} members, how would you compute monthly benefit cost against revenue, and what is recomputed when a refund arrives late?

rules.ask: A single status column says "active". How do you answer how many members were in grace on the 3rd of last month, and why an order from that day got the benefit?
A member cancels on the 10th with the period paid to the 25th. What does your expiry say on the 12th, and does an order on the 20th get the benefit?
The subtotal was {{min_subtotal}} before a promotion and below it after. Which number does your benefit decision store, and could you reproduce the decision a year later?
An annual plan was paid in March. How does monthly revenue report it, and what happens when it is refunded in May?
Which events in this exercise prorate, and where is the prorated amount stored so finance can reconcile it with the charges?

incidents: After a payment provider outage, thousands of renewals failed at once. A version that ended memberships on the first failed attempt removed benefits from members who were still inside this exercise's grace period, and support received complaints about delivery fees.
The monthly benefit cost doubled for one week: orders that were edited after placement recorded a second benefit decision, and the report summed both.
Members who started a {{trial_days}}-day trial late in the evening were charged a day early: the trial end was computed in UTC days while the member had been shown a local date.

templates.title: Ordered while closed — orders accepted while a store was paused or outside its listed hours, and open minutes lost to pauses, per store and week
templates.subtopic: holiday overrides of weekly hours, intervals across midnight, half-open boundaries, three-way interval intersection, store-week calendars

sections.scenario: A local commerce marketplace lists each store's hours, and a merchant can pause a store from its tablet or portal when the kitchen is overwhelmed or the tablet is offline (this exercise's model; check current docs for how real merchant tools behave). An order should not be accepted while a store is paused or outside its listed hours, yet some are: an app showing a stale menu, a clock out of step, a scheduled order. Merchant operations want a weekly view per store: how many orders were accepted while the store was closed, how many of those during a pause, and how many open minutes each store lost to pauses. {{sample_note}} The sample covers {{weeks}} weeks, from Monday {{first_day}} to Sunday {{last_day}}, for {{store_count}} stores.
sections.problem:
Write one PostgreSQL query that returns store_id, week_start, orders_accepted, orders_while_closed, orders_while_paused, minutes_paused: one row for every store and every week of the sample, zeros included, ordered by store_id, week_start.

  • week_start is the Monday of the week; a week runs from Monday 00:00 to the next Monday 00:00. An order belongs to the week of its accepted_at.
  • Listed hours for a date. If the store has any holiday_hours rows for that date, they replace the date's weekly hours entirely, and a row with NULL times means closed all day. Otherwise the store's weekly_hours rows for the date's ISO weekday (1 = Monday … 7 = Sunday) apply; a weekday with no rows is closed.
  • Each listed row is the interval [date + open_time, date + close_time). When close_time is earlier than open_time, the interval ends at close_time on the next date. Hours belong to the date they open on: an interval that opened the evening before still applies after midnight, even when the new date is a holiday or the first day of the sample.
  • A pause is [paused_at, resumed_at). A NULL resumed_at means the store was still paused at {{sample_end}}, the end of the sample.
  • orders_while_closed counts orders accepted while the store was paused or outside its listed hours, each order once. orders_while_paused counts orders accepted while it was paused.
  • minutes_paused is the number of minutes in the week during which the store was both paused and inside its listed hours, as an integer. A pause that crosses Monday 00:00 is split between the two weeks, and minutes before {{first_day}} are outside the sample.
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Every timestamp is a TIMESTAMP (without time zone) in the stores' local time; the stores share one time zone and the sample has no daylight-saving change, so no conversion is needed. A store's listed intervals never overlap each other, and neither do its pauses. Pause boundaries fall on whole minutes. You may use {{first_day}}, {{last_day}} and {{sample_end}} as literals. The sample has {{order_rows}} orders; production has hundreds of thousands of stores and runs this report every Monday morning.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical schema, stores, hours, pauses and orders. The hours, holiday and pause rules are this exercise's model. An order that was accepted and later cancelled still counts as accepted here.
sections.criteria: Listed intervals built per store and date, with holiday rows replacing weekly rows and NULL rows meaning closed; intervals across midnight kept whole and taken from the day before the sample; half-open boundaries for hours and pauses; an open pause ended at the end of the sample; orders while closed counted once; paused minutes from a three-way intersection clipped to each week; every store-week present with zeros; deterministic order; can discuss time zones and daylight saving, overlapping pauses, cause attribution and materialisation.

clarifications.q: An order accepted exactly at close_time?
clarifications.a: The store was closed. Intervals are half-open: open from open_time, closed from close_time.

clarifications.q: A late-night store is open 17:00 to 01:30, and Wednesday is a holiday when it is closed all day. Is it open at 00:45 on Wednesday?
