clarifications.a: Yes. Tuesday's interval opened on Tuesday and runs to 01:30 on Wednesday; Wednesday's holiday replaces only the hours that open on Wednesday.

clarifications.q: Does a pause outside listed hours count towards minutes_paused?
clarifications.a: No, only the minutes when the store would otherwise have been open. An order accepted during such a pause still counts as accepted while paused.

clarifications.q: A store had no orders in a week.
clarifications.a: It still gets a row, with zero orders and whatever paused minutes it had.

clarifications.q: An order is accepted during a pause and after closing time.
clarifications.a: It counts once in orders_while_closed and once in orders_while_paused.

hints: Build the listed intervals first: one row per store and date from {{first_day}} − 1 through {{last_day}} (generate_series), joined to that date's holiday rows when it has any (dropping the NULL ones) and otherwise to the weekly rows (NOT EXISTS). date + time gives a timestamp; add a day to the close when it is earlier than the open.
Flag each order with EXISTS (a pause contains it) and NOT EXISTS (a listed interval contains it), then count with FILTER.

For the minutes, intersect three intervals — the pause, the listed interval and the week — with GREATEST of the starts and LEAST of the ends, keep the positive pieces, and sum EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM …) / 60.
Start the final SELECT from stores crossed with weeks and LEFT JOIN both aggregates.
followups: Stores sit in several time zones and the sample crosses a daylight-saving change. What changes in the schema and in the query, and which "minutes" are right on the night the clocks go back?
Two pauses of one store overlap (the tablet and the portal both paused it). What does your query report, and how would you make it correct?
Merchants want orders while closed split by cause: paused, outside weekly hours, closed for a holiday. How do you attribute an order with more than one cause?
At production scale, rebuilding every store's intervals for every date each week is wasteful. What would you materialise, at what grain, and what invalidates it?

rules.ask: BETWEEN includes both ends. What does your query say about an order accepted exactly at close_time, or exactly at resumed_at?
Which store-weeks disappear when you start from the orders, and what about a week that had paused minutes but no orders?
Tuesday's interval opens at 17:00 and closes at 01:30, and Wednesday is a holiday closed all day. Is the store open at 00:45 on Wednesday in your query?
An order accepted during a pause after closing time. How many times does your orders_while_closed count it?
How do you keep a pause's minutes before {{first_day}}, or beyond the end of the week, out of the sum?
A pause with no resumed_at: why end it at the end of the sample rather than now, and what would rerunning last month's report give otherwise?

incidents: A late-night store showed about a third of its orders as accepted outside its hours every week: a version of this query cut every interval at midnight, so each order after 00:00 looked closed.
Merchants who set holiday hours for a date saw their previous night's late orders flagged as closed: holiday rows were applied from midnight and cut short the evening before.
A few stores showed thousands of paused minutes: automatic pauses from tablets that never reconnected had no resumed_at, and the report counted them to the end of the period without anyone checking.

templates.title: Item availability for convenience and grocery: pick outcomes, merchant feeds and honest freshness
templates.subtopic: signal fusion, a given score, freshness decay, calibration

sections.scenario: A local commerce marketplace lists {{stores}} convenience and grocery stores next to its restaurants, each store listing about {{listings}} items. What the marketplace knows about whether an item is on the shelf comes from several places: inventory feeds from merchants (a full file every {{feed_hours}} hours, and from some merchants small updates in between), pick outcomes recorded while an order is shopped (found, found with fewer units, substituted, not found) at up to {{peak_picks}} per second at peak, the merchant marking an item out of stock in its tools, and consumers reporting a missing item after delivery. You are given a scoring function that takes recent evidence for one store-item and returns the probability that the item is on the shelf now. Consumers browse store pages and search results that show each item as in stock, likely limited, or out of stock. Showing an item as in stock that is then not found leads to substitutions, refunds and a disappointed consumer; hiding an item that is there loses the sale.
sections.problem: Design the system that turns these signals into the availability state consumers see. Cover ingestion of each kind of signal; the evidence kept per store-item; when the scoring function is called, with what inputs, and how its output becomes a displayed state; what the page says about how recent the evidence is; how the state reaches store pages and search; how a merchant's explicit out-of-stock mark overrides everything else; and how you measure whether the states you show are honest.
sections.constraints: An item the merchant marks out of stock must leave consumer view within 60 seconds. A not-found pick must be reflected in that store's displayed state within 2 minutes. Store page reads p99 under 30 ms. The displayed state never claims more certainty than the evidence supports: an item with no evidence for days is shown as unconfirmed, not as in stock. Pick outcomes are store-item evidence only; they are never attributed to, reported by, or used to evaluate the person who shopped the order.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, timings, thresholds and rules are hypothetical. The scoring function is given and is not yours to design: its inputs are the time since the item was last found and last not found, the latest feed quantity and its age, the item's typical sales rate in that store, and the store's local hour; its output is a probability. Merchants differ greatly in how reliable their feeds are.
sections.criteria: Separates the evidence log from derived state, with idempotent ingestion per signal type and store-item ordering; the given score called with explicit evidence and cached with the time it is valid until, plus scheduled re-evaluation as evidence ages; a stated mapping from score to displayed state, with an honest unconfirmed state and freshness shown; merchant out-of-stock marks as a fast override path with cache invalidation; per-merchant feed reliability measured and used; calibration and shown-in-stock-but-not-found metrics in aggregate per store, never per person; safe rollout of a new score version (shadow scoring, comparing calibration); adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Do I design the scoring model?
clarifications.a: No. It is a function you are given. You decide when it is called, with which evidence, how its output is cached, and how it maps to what consumers see.

clarifications.q: How reliable are merchant feeds?
clarifications.a: Some are accurate, some are hours stale, and a few report every item as in stock. Treat each merchant's feed as having a measured reliability.

clarifications.q: Is an out-of-stock item hidden or shown greyed?
clarifications.a: Your call. Say what each choice does to search, to substitutions and to consumers who come back later.

clarifications.q: Can a consumer order an item shown as likely limited?
clarifications.a: Yes; checkout asks for a substitution preference for it.

clarifications.q: Who can see pick outcomes?
clarifications.a: Only as aggregated store-item evidence. There is no view of them by shopper or courier.

hints: Keep an append-only log of evidence per store-item and treat the displayed state as a projection of it plus the clock; then a state can always be recomputed and explained.

Evidence goes stale even when nothing happens. Instead of rescoring every item every minute, compute when each item's state would next change if no new evidence arrives, and schedule a re-evaluation for that moment.
Honesty is measurable: of the items shown as in stock when an order was placed, what share were found at pick time? Track it per store and per state.
followups: Walk one not-found pick from the shopping app to the item changing state on the next consumer's page. Where is the time spent?
The merchant feed says 40 units on hand, and the item was not found on three orders in the last hour. What does the consumer see, and why?
How do you keep {{stores}} stores of about {{listings}} listings each up to date as evidence ages, without rescoring everything every minute?
The shown-in-stock-but-not-found rate differs widely between stores. How do you measure it fairly and act on it, without it becoming a judgement of any person?
You are given a new version of the scoring function. How do you roll it out and prove the states it produces are at least as honest?

rules.ask: A merchant marks an item out of stock. How long do your cached store pages and search results keep showing it, and what invalidates them?
A popular item sells out at 18:00. How long until consumers stop seeing it as in stock in your design, and how many orders meet a not-found pick in the meantime?
How do you guarantee that pick outcomes stay store-item evidence and never become a view of one person's performance?
Who chooses the thresholds between in stock, likely limited and out of stock, and which metric tells you they are wrong?
The partition for one large chain's stores falls 20 minutes behind at peak. What do consumers of those stores see, and does the page say so?

incidents: After a chain changes its point-of-sale export, its feed reports every listing in all its stores as in stock with a quantity of 999. Within a day, not-found picks for that chain triple.

At the evening peak, pick outcomes reach {{peak_picks}} per second, the scoring function's p99 rises to 2 seconds, the evidence queue backs up, and displayed states for evening orders are 25 minutes old.
Over a holiday weekend, the feeds of several stores, normally sent every {{feed_hours}} hours, stop arriving for 30 hours. Their items keep showing as in stock with no new evidence.

templates.title: Consumer promotions: eligibility, real-time budgets, redemption caps and reconciled accounting
templates.subtopic: rule evaluation, budget counters, caps, redemption ledger

sections.scenario: A local commerce marketplace runs {{campaigns}} active consumer promotions at any time: percentage and fixed discounts on an order, free delivery, and item-level offers. Some are funded by the marketplace, some by merchants for their own stores. Each has eligibility rules (new consumers only, members only, certain stores or cities, a minimum subtotal, certain hours), a total budget, and a cap on redemptions per consumer. Promotions combine by this exercise's stacking rule: at most one marketplace-funded and one merchant-funded promotion on an order, and the membership delivery-fee benefit is applied separately. A flagship campaign this weekend is funded with {{budget}}, allows at most {{per_consumer_cap}} redemptions per consumer, and checkouts peak at {{peak_checkouts}} per second.
sections.problem: Design the promotions platform. Cover how campaigns and their rules are defined, versioned and validated; how eligible promotions are found and evaluated for a cart quickly; how the best allowed combination is chosen under the stacking rule; how budgets and per-consumer caps are enforced as redemptions happen; what happens when an order is cancelled, refunded or changed after a promotion was applied; and the redemption accounting that finance and merchants reconcile against completed orders.
sections.constraints: Cart pricing including promotions p99 under 150 ms. A campaign's spend may exceed its budget by at most 1%, and a consumer may never exceed the per-consumer cap. The discount a consumer was shown at checkout is the discount charged, unless the consumer is told before placing the order. Every discount on every order must be traceable to a campaign version and a funder. Merchants see only redemptions for their own stores.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, budgets, rules and timings are hypothetical; stacking, eligibility and refund rules are this exercise's rules (check current docs). Orders are priced by a separate cart service that calls you; payment is authorised after pricing and can fail.
sections.criteria: Campaigns as versioned, validated rule definitions with dry runs; a precompiled eligibility index so a cart meets few candidates; combination selection under the stacking rule with deterministic ties; budget enforcement with an explicit tolerance (allotments, reserve-then-commit, or a single writer per campaign) and exact per-consumer caps keyed by consumer and campaign; a redemption ledger of reserve, commit and release entries keyed by order and campaign version, with idempotent retries; post-order changes (cancellation, partial refund, edits) mapped to ledger entries by rule; reconciliation against completed orders and per-merchant statements; abuse handled in general terms (velocity limits per campaign, budget pacing guards) without evasion detail; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: When does a redemption count against the budget, at pricing or at order placement?
clarifications.a: Your call. Say what happens to the budget when a priced cart is abandoned, and when a placed order is cancelled.

clarifications.q: Is the budget measured in redemptions or in money?
clarifications.a: In money: the sum of discounts given. Discounts vary by order.

clarifications.q: Does a cancelled order give the redemption back?
clarifications.a: By this exercise's rule, a full cancellation before the store accepts returns both the budget and the consumer's redemption; later cancellations return neither.

clarifications.q: Can a merchant change a running campaign?
clarifications.a: It can raise the budget or end the campaign early; other changes create a new version for future orders only.

clarifications.q: Who decides which combination a consumer gets?
clarifications.a: The best combination for the consumer that the stacking rule allows, with ties broken by a stated rule.

hints: Precompile campaigns into an index by store, city and audience so a cart is evaluated against a few dozen candidates, not {{campaigns}}.
A budget is a counter decremented by thousands of checkouts. Split it into allotments with a reserve, or let it be slightly approximate within the allowed 1%, and say which.
Treat redemptions as a ledger of reserve, commit and release entries keyed by order; budgets, caps and finance reports are projections of it.
followups: Walk one checkout for the flagship campaign: which records change, in what order, and what keeps the consumer's {{per_consumer_cap}}-redemption cap exact when the same consumer checks out from two devices at once?
The budget has 2% left and checkouts run at {{peak_checkouts}} per second. How do you stop at the budget without making consumers who saw the discount lose it at payment?
An order is partly refunded after delivery because one item was missing. What happens to the discount, the budget, and the merchant's statement?
Finance finds that the redemption ledger and the discounts on completed orders differ by 0.3% for last month. How do you find which orders explain it?
A merchant-funded campaign and a marketplace campaign both apply. How do you prove to the merchant exactly what its campaign cost and why?

rules.ask: The node holding the flagship budget counter fails at peak. What does the replacement start from, and how do you know the campaign has not overspent?
Every checkout for the flagship campaign takes the same budget row lock. What is the p99 pricing latency at {{peak_checkouts}} per second?
Which of your numbers may be eventually consistent, the budget, the per-consumer cap or the ledger, and which must be exact?
A campaign manager writes a rule that makes every order in a city eligible by mistake. What catches it before it goes live?
The refund arrives three weeks after the campaign ended and its budget was closed. Where does that entry go?

incidents: The flagship campaign's {{budget}} budget is overspent by 18% in the first hour: carts priced before the budget ran out kept being placed for several minutes afterwards, and each was honoured.

A promotion code is shared widely; redemptions for it jump 40-fold in an hour, mostly from accounts created that day. The per-consumer cap of {{per_consumer_cap}} holds, but the budget drains before regular consumers can use it.
Month-end reconciliation shows redemptions committed for orders cancelled before the store accepted them were never released; the ledger is 0.7% above the discounts on completed orders.

templates.title: Merchant analytics portal: hourly store results, each merchant seeing only its own
templates.subtopic: hourly refresh, row-level access, restatement, aggregation thresholds

sections.scenario: {{merchants}} merchants use a web portal to see how their stores are doing on a local commerce marketplace that handles about {{daily_orders}} orders a day. For each store they see sales, orders and average order value; item performance (top items, items often reported missing, items often unavailable); order accuracy (orders with a missing or incorrect item reported); ratings and reviews; and the results of promotions they funded (redemptions, sales on promoted orders, what the promotion cost them). Numbers are shown by hour and day in each store's local time, with {{history_months}} months of history. Merchants range from a single restaurant to a chain of {{chain_stores}} stores, some run by franchise owners who should see only the stores they own.
sections.problem: Design the data system behind the portal. Cover the sources and how they arrive; the models and aggregates; the hourly refresh; how late corrections (refunds, accuracy reports and ratings that arrive days later) change past numbers and how merchants are told; access control so that every user sees exactly the stores they are allowed to; and the serving layer that makes the portal fast.
sections.constraints: Data at most 90 minutes old during the day. Dashboard queries p95 under 2 seconds, including for the largest chains over a year. No merchant may ever see another merchant's data, and a franchise owner or store manager sees only the stores assigned to them. Consumers appear only in aggregate; reviews are shown as consumers published them, without identifiers. Courier-related issues appear only as store-level aggregates and never identify a courier. Promotion results are reported as observed, with no claim of incremental lift.
sections.assumptions: All volumes and timings are hypothetical. Order, item, refund, rating and promotion events arrive in a central log within minutes; some corrections arrive days later. A merchant's organisation, its stores and its users' roles are kept in a separate account service that changes during the day.
sections.criteria: Event log to modelled facts (orders, items, refunds, accuracy reports, ratings, redemptions) keyed by order and store, with each store's local day and hour computed at ingestion; incremental hourly aggregates per store and local hour, with merchant and day rollups for chains; one central access rule driven by current assignments (row-level security or an access-checked query layer) applied to caches and exports alike; a restatement policy with versioned numbers, labelled changes and a closing window; aggregation thresholds and no consumer or courier identifiers; promotion results as observed without lift claims; backfills isolated from the hourly path; an access audit log; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Which time zone are the numbers in?
clarifications.a: Each store's local time. A chain's total across time zones is the sum of each store's local days.

clarifications.q: Can past numbers change?
clarifications.a: Yes; refunds, missing-item reports and ratings arrive late. Say how merchants learn that a number they saw has changed.

clarifications.q: What can a store manager see?
clarifications.a: Only their assigned stores, and only some metrics; owners see everything for the stores they own.

clarifications.q: Are reviews shown with names?
clarifications.a: As the consumer published them, with no identifiers beyond that; filtering and aggregates only above a minimum count.

clarifications.q: Do merchants export data?
clarifications.a: Yes, as files of their own stores' daily results.

hints: Pre-aggregate per store and local hour; chains read many small aggregates, so think about rollups per merchant and per day as well.
Put the access rule in one place that every query passes through, keyed by the user's current store assignments, not in each dashboard.
Decide a restatement policy: which windows may change, how a changed number is labelled, and how long numbers stay open.
followups: Walk one order from placement to appearing in its store's hourly sales. Where is the time spent, and what is the hour it belongs to?
A chain of {{chain_stores}} stores opens a year-long view. What is precomputed and what is computed at query time to stay under 2 seconds?
A store moves from one franchise owner to another at noon. Who sees which hours of that day, and what enforces it?
A missing-item report arrives four days after the order and changes last week's order accuracy. What does the merchant see?
How would you prove to an auditor that no merchant saw another merchant's data last quarter?

rules.ask: The account service changes a user's store assignments. How quickly does your row-level rule pick it up, and what does the user see in between?
A refund for an order from five weeks ago arrives. Which rollups change, and how much do you recompute?
A store closes at 02:00 local time. Which day do its last orders belong to, and on the night clocks change?
A cached chain-level result includes a store the user lost access to an hour ago. What stops it from being served?
An export includes reviews. What stops it from carrying consumer identifiers the portal never shows?

incidents: A store transfers between franchise owners in a chain of {{chain_stores}} stores; for two days the previous owner can still see the store's sales because a cached permission list was not refreshed.
A schema change requires backfilling {{history_months}} months of item performance. The backfill competes with the hourly refresh, and by 18:00 dashboards show data as of 13:00.
A merchant notices that last week's order accuracy changed between Monday and Thursday with no notice; late missing-item reports were applied silently.

templates.title: Dish search in a delivery area: open now, menu hours and fresh menus
templates.subtopic: geo filtering, time-dependent eligibility, incremental indexing

sections.scenario: Consumers on a local commerce marketplace search for a dish ("pad thai", "gluten-free pizza", "oat milk latte") and expect stores and items that can actually be delivered to them now. The index holds {{stores_in_index}} stores and {{items_indexed}} menu items. Each store delivers to an area that is not a simple circle, keeps weekly hours that may cross midnight plus holiday hours and temporary pauses, and may have menus that apply only at certain hours (breakfast until 11:00, a late-night menu). Items can be unavailable. Merchants change menus all day and expect a change to be searchable within {{freshness_minutes}} minutes. Search traffic peaks at {{qps}} queries per second around meal times. Ordering of the results is done by a relevance scoring function you are given.
sections.problem: Design dish search. Cover how stores, menus and items are indexed (and how dish words are matched, including synonyms and spelling variations); how the delivery area filter works for a consumer's location; how open-now, menu hours, holiday hours, pauses and item availability are applied at query time; how menu, hours and availability changes flow into the index within {{freshness_minutes}} minutes; the serving path at {{qps}} queries per second; and how you know the results are correct (no closed stores, no unavailable items, no menus outside their hours).
sections.constraints: Search p99 under 200 ms. A store that is closed or paused, or an item that is unavailable or outside its menu hours, must not appear as orderable. Hours are in each store's local time, including on the days clocks change and across midnight. A merchant's pause must take effect in search within 60 seconds.
sections.assumptions: All volumes and timings are hypothetical. Menus, hours and availability come from other services as change events; the relevance scoring function is given and needs only the candidate set and a few features. Delivery areas are polygons that change a few times a week.
sections.criteria: An index of stores and items with dish matching (analysers, synonyms by locale, spelling tolerance) and a separation between slow document fields and fast fields (availability, pause, hours) updated in place; delivery areas precomputed to grid cells with an exact edge check; open-now and menu hours evaluated correctly in local time (a compact weekly schedule at query time, or transition-driven field updates) including midnight crossings, holidays, pauses and DST; change events into the index with priority for pauses and availability, and backpressure for bulk menu replaces; sharding by geography with replicas for meal-time peaks; checkout re-validation as the final guard; continuous correctness probes (synthetic searches against the source of truth); adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Do I design the ranking?
clarifications.a: No. You produce the set of eligible candidates and their features; the given function orders them.

clarifications.q: Can a closed store appear at all?
clarifications.a: It can appear as "opens at 17:00" if you choose, but never as orderable now.

clarifications.q: Is "open now" evaluated at index time or query time?
clarifications.a: Your choice. Say what each costs at the moment a store opens or closes.

clarifications.q: How are delivery areas defined?
clarifications.a: Polygons per store, which can be large in suburbs and small in dense cities.

clarifications.q: Do scheduled orders search for a future time?
clarifications.a: Yes, sometimes. The same filters then apply at the chosen time.

hints: Hours change state at known moments. Either evaluate a compact weekly schedule at query time in the store's time zone, or update a small "orderable now" field at each transition; avoid reindexing whole menus.
Map delivery-area polygons to a grid of cells at index time, so a consumer's location becomes one cell lookup plus an exact check for edge cells.
Separate slow-changing documents (item names, descriptions) from fast-changing fields (availability, pause, hours) so the fast ones can be updated in place.
followups: Walk one merchant menu change, a new item, from the merchant's tool to the first search that returns it. Where is the time spent?
A consumer searches at 10:59 for an item on a breakfast menu that ends at 11:00, and places the order at 11:02. What happens?
How do you shard {{items_indexed}} items so a query for one location touches only a few shards, and what is hot at meal times?
A large chain replaces its whole menu in 3,000 stores at 11:30, just before lunch. How does the index keep up, and what do searchers see meanwhile?
How do you continuously measure that no closed store, unavailable item or out-of-hours menu is shown as orderable?

rules.ask: A store's delivery area covers part of a cell. How do you avoid showing it to a consumer just outside the area?
A store toggles 200 items' availability in a minute. How do you update them without reindexing whole documents?
A store's hours are 18:00 to 02:00. On the night clocks go back, when is it open in your design?
Search results are cached for popular queries. A store pauses; how long do cached results show it as orderable?
"Pop" and "soda" mean the same thing in some regions and not others. Where do synonyms live, and who can change them?

incidents: On the night clocks go back, stores whose hours cross midnight show as closed in search for an hour while their tablets accept orders.
A large chain replaces its whole menu in 3,000 stores at 11:30. The index update backlog grows, and menu changes take 40 minutes to become searchable instead of {{freshness_minutes}}.
Breakfast items keep appearing until 11:15 after the breakfast menu ends at 11:00; orders placed for them are cancelled by the store.

templates.title: Scheduled and group orders: days ahead, many participants, re-checked at fulfilment
templates.subtopic: deferred execution, shared carts, re-validation, payment splits

sections.scenario: On a local commerce marketplace, consumers can schedule an order up to {{days_ahead}} days ahead for a chosen delivery time, and can start a group order: the host shares a link, up to {{group_size}} participants add their own items to one cart until a deadline {{join_deadline_minutes}} minutes after it opens, and then the host places the order. The host either pays for everything or each participant pays for their own items (this exercise's rule). At 12:00 on a weekday, {{peak_scheduled}} scheduled orders are due across the marketplace. Between placement and fulfilment, things change: a store edits its hours or adds a holiday closure, items become unavailable, prices and promotions change, and payment authorisations can expire.
sections.problem: Design scheduled and group orders. Cover how a scheduled order is stored and when it is released to the store (and what is re-checked at release: store hours, pauses, item availability, prices, promotions, payment); how a group cart handles many participants editing at once and the deadline; who is charged for what, including fees, promotions, the membership fee benefit and taxes, under this exercise's rules; what consumers are told when something changes before fulfilment; and how the release path survives {{peak_scheduled}} orders due at the same minute.
sections.constraints: A scheduled order must reach the store early enough for its preparation time and never after the store has closed. Consumers are never charged more than the amount they confirmed without being asked first. In a group order paid per participant, no participant pays for another's items. Release-time checks must complete for all orders due at a peak minute within 2 minutes. Courier assignment is out of scope; treat it as a service that receives a released order.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, timings and rules are hypothetical; fee, promotion, membership and refund rules are this exercise's rules (check current docs). By this exercise's rule an authorisation is valid for 7 days, so orders scheduled further ahead are authorised again near release. Each store states a preparation time per order size.
sections.criteria: Scheduled orders as a durable state machine with a computed release time, a timer index, and exactly-once release (leases and idempotent transitions); release-time re-validation of hours, holiday closures, pauses, availability, prices, promotions and payment with each change recorded as a decision and communicated; early detection when hours change after scheduling (re-checking affected orders when a store edits its hours, not only at release); peak release planned ahead with pre-checks and smoothing; group carts as per-participant sub-carts locked at the deadline, with clear payment split rules for fees, promotions, the membership benefit, taxes and remainder cents; never charging more than confirmed without consent; an auditable charge breakdown per person; no dispatch design; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Is the price fixed when a scheduled order is placed?
clarifications.a: By this exercise's rule, the consumer pays the price shown when they placed it, unless an item's price went up by more than 10%, in which case they are asked.

clarifications.q: What if an item is unavailable at release?
clarifications.a: The consumer's substitution preference applies; with none, the item is removed and refunded, and the consumer is told.

clarifications.q: Can participants edit after the host places the group order?
clarifications.a: No. Until the deadline they can edit their own items only.

clarifications.q: Who gets the membership fee benefit in a group order?
clarifications.a: By this exercise's rule, the host's membership applies to the whole order when the host pays; when each pays their own share, delivery fees are split equally and each member's share is waived.

clarifications.q: Can a store refuse scheduled orders?
clarifications.a: It can limit how many it accepts per hour; say how that limit is honoured.

hints: A scheduled order is a state machine with a release time (due time minus preparation time minus a margin); a durable timer index by release minute turns the 12:00 peak into a planned batch you can start early.
Re-check at release against the same sources checkout uses; anything that changed becomes an explicit decision recorded on the order.
A group cart is many writers on one document. Give each participant their own sub-cart and lock them all at the deadline, rather than letting everyone edit one list.
followups: Walk one order scheduled {{days_ahead}} days ahead from placement to release. Which records change, and what is re-checked when?
{{peak_scheduled}} scheduled orders are due at 12:00. How do you release them on time without a thundering herd on store hours, availability and payments?
In a group order paid per participant, one participant's card declines after the deadline. What happens to the order and to everyone else?
A store adds a holiday closure for tomorrow after hundreds of orders were scheduled into it. What does the system do, and what do consumers see?
How do you prove, for any order, exactly what each person was charged and why, months later?

rules.ask: The scheduler node handling the 11:30 releases restarts at 11:29. How do you guarantee each order is released exactly once and on time?
Forty participants add items in the last minute before the deadline. What do they experience under your concurrency control?
An order is scheduled {{days_ahead}} days ahead. When is the payment authorised, and what happens if the second authorisation fails at release?
Which states can an order move back from, and who can trigger each transition?
A promotion of $10 off applies to a group order paid per participant. Who gets how much of it, and how is the remainder cent assigned?

incidents: A store enters a holiday closure the evening before; the next day 300 scheduled orders due during the closure are released to it and are cancelled by the store at release.

The release job for 12:00 starts late at 11:52; {{peak_scheduled}} orders are re-checked at once, the availability service throttles, and a quarter of the orders reach stores after their preparation time began.
In a group order of {{group_size}} participants paid per participant, an item became unavailable after a participant added it; the participant is charged for it and the item is refunded a day later.

templates.title: A statistically significant result too small to matter, and the launch pressure behind it
templates.subtopic: practical significance, guardrails, influencing a launch decision

change: a new substitution prompt in grocery checkout
cost: two engineers maintaining a second code path for a year
a 3% increase in page load time on older phones
a new dependency on a service with no on-call coverage at night

sections.scenario: Your team ran a three-week experiment on {{change}} with {{sample}}. The result is {{lift}}, statistically significant at the threshold the team agreed beforehand. The product manager and their director want to announce the launch at next week's quarterly review, where the change is already on the slide. You own the experimentation data and the analysis. Looking closely, you believe the effect is too small to matter for the business, the confidence interval reaches almost to zero, one guardrail metric (orders with a missing-item report) moved slightly in the wrong direction without reaching significance, and shipping it brings {{cost}}.
sections.problem: What do you do? Cover how you check your own analysis before saying anything, how you frame the result so people can decide (not only "significant" or "not"), how you raise it with the product manager and the director given the timing, what you recommend, and what you would put in place so the next experiment has its decision rule agreed before it starts. Then tell me about a real time a result you analysed was used to justify a decision you disagreed with, with what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You are not the decision maker; the product manager and director are. The review is in a week. The experiment cannot be rerun before then.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Checks the analysis first (sample ratio, novelty effects, segment consistency, the interval rather than the point estimate); translates the lift into absolute business terms and weighs it against {{cost}} with uncertainty; separates significance from practical importance and from guardrail risk, and states what the experiment could and could not detect; raises it early with the product manager, then the director together, before the review; offers options (launch, partial launch with a holdout and a stated decision rule, do not launch, simplify the change to remove the cost); accepts the decision makers' call while making the residual risk visible; proposes pre-registered decision rules (minimum effect worth shipping, guardrail thresholds, power) for future experiments; real example with personal contribution and outcome, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Was a minimum effect worth shipping agreed before the experiment?
clarifications.a: No. Only the significance threshold was agreed.

clarifications.q: Is the guardrail movement real?
clarifications.a: Unknown. It is within noise, but the experiment was not sized to detect a change of that size in that metric.

clarifications.q: Does the director know about the cost?
clarifications.a: Not in detail; the launch slide lists only the lift.

clarifications.q: Can the launch be partial?
clarifications.a: Yes. It could ship to a share of traffic or a set of cities.

hints: Translate the lift into what it means in absolute terms (orders per week, money per year) and compare it with the cost, both with their uncertainty.
Separate three questions: is the effect real, is it large enough to matter, and is anything getting worse.
Give the decision makers options with consequences, not a verdict; and give them time before the review, not during it.
followups: Show me how you would present {{lift}} to the director in one slide: what numbers, what uncertainty, what comparison.
The product manager says "significant is significant, and we committed to shipping something this quarter." How do you respond?
What would make you change your mind and support the launch as it is?
How would you set up the next experiment so this argument happens before it starts, not after?
In your real example, what did you personally do, and how was the decision made in the end?

rules.ask: Statistical significance answers whether the effect is likely non-zero. What answers whether it is worth shipping?
The guardrail moved in the wrong direction but not significantly. Was the experiment able to detect a change that would matter there? How do you know?
How do you raise this with the director without going around the product manager?
You propose a partial launch with a holdout. What decides, and when, whether it goes to everyone or is removed?
What did you personally say, to whom, and when?

templates.title: Replacing the spreadsheets an operations team runs the business on
templates.subtopic: migrating manual workflows, trust, adoption

team: the regional operations team that onboards new stores
the team that plans merchant-funded promotion budgets each week
the team that tracks store hours and holiday closures for a region

sections.scenario: The work of {{team}} runs on {{sheets}} linked spreadsheets that {{people}} people edit every day. The spreadsheets hold reference data, manual overrides and formulas that feed decisions other teams rely on; several have broken after someone sorted a column or pasted over a formula, and twice a wrong value reached consumers or merchants before anyone noticed. You have been asked to replace them with a proper system within {{months}} months. The team is proud of the spreadsheets, knows them better than anyone, and is wary: an earlier tool imposed on them slowed them down and was abandoned.
sections.problem: How would you lead this? Cover how you learn what the spreadsheets actually do (including the parts nobody documented), how you involve the team that uses them, what you build first, how you migrate without stopping their work, how you know the new system gives the same or better answers, and when and how the spreadsheets are retired. Then tell me about a real time you replaced a manual process people depended on, with what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: The operations team's work cannot pause. You have two engineers and part of an analyst's time. The team's manager supports the project but will not force adoption.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Learns the work by observing it and inventories the spreadsheets by the decisions they support, not by their cells; involves the operations team as co-owners (named people, regular reviews, their acceptance criteria); prioritises the workflow with the most incidents or toil and migrates it end to end; extracts hidden rules into tested, documented logic, with validation that prevents the past incidents; runs old and new in parallel with output comparison, explaining every difference; retires spreadsheets explicitly with a date and read-only archives, while allowing safe exploration; handles opposition by listening and giving the opponent a real role; measures success by incidents and time saved; real example with personal contribution and outcome, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Does anyone understand all the spreadsheets?
clarifications.a: No single person. Two long-serving team members understand most of them.

clarifications.q: Are all the spreadsheets worth keeping?
clarifications.a: Probably not; some are copies, and some are no longer used.

clarifications.q: Can the team keep a spreadsheet for exploration afterwards?
clarifications.a: Your call; say what you would allow and why.

clarifications.q: What does success look like to the team's manager?
clarifications.a: No more incidents from broken formulas, and less time spent on manual checks.

hints: Watch the work before designing anything: sit with the people who use the spreadsheets and list the decisions they support.
Migrate one workflow end to end and let the team judge it, rather than building a full replacement first.
Run old and new side by side and compare outputs; differences are either bugs or undocumented rules worth knowing.
followups: How do you find the rules hidden in formulas and manual habits that nobody wrote down?
Which workflow do you migrate first, and why that one?
Two months in, half the team uses the new system and half still uses the spreadsheets, and their numbers differ. What do you do?
One of the two long-serving team members opposes the change openly. How do you handle it?
In your real example, what did the people who did the work by hand teach you that changed your design?

rules.ask: The team says the spreadsheet "just works" and cannot list requirements. How do you get them anyway?
What happens on cutover day if the new system gives a different answer for a store than the spreadsheet did?
People still copy data out of the new system into a spreadsheet. Is that a failure? What does it tell you?
Which manual checks would you deliberately keep human, and why?
Which decisions were yours, and which did the operations team make?

templates.title: Scope that keeps growing after the plan and the date were agreed
templates.subtopic: scope control, trade-offs, communicating with sponsors

project: holiday hours support in merchant tools
an annual billing option for the membership subscription
a daily reporting export for merchants who use white-label delivery
added: three requests from the team that supports the largest merchants
rules for two more countries added by a regional lead
a redesign of the report layout requested by product design

sections.scenario: You lead {{team_size}} engineers building {{project}}. The scope and the launch date were agreed with the sponsors six weeks ago, and the date has been announced to merchants. With {{weeks_left}} weeks left, the work has grown: {{added}}, plus a steady trickle of small "while you are in there" changes. Each request is reasonable on its own. Together they add about 40% to the remaining work, and the team has started working evenings to keep up. Nobody has said the date can move.
sections.problem: What do you do? Cover how you find out how much the scope has actually grown and what it does to the date, how you present the trade-off and to whom, how you decide what goes in, what is deferred and what is dropped, how you protect the team, and how new requests are handled from now on. Then tell me about a real project whose scope grew after it was agreed, with what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: The date was announced to merchants. You cannot add people in time to help. You do not own the sponsors' priorities.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Quantifies the growth against the agreed baseline with sources and sizes; raises the trade-off early and explicitly with the sponsors who agreed the scope, with options and a recommendation (cut, defer, phase, or move the date with reasons), rather than absorbing it; checks the claimed launch-critical addition with evidence; communicates deferrals to requesters directly; protects the team (stops the evening work as a plan, makes it visible, sustainable pace) and introduces an intake rule with a named decision maker; keeps merchants' expectations accurate if the release is phased; real example with personal contribution and outcome, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Who agreed the original scope?
clarifications.a: The product lead and the head of merchant operations, with you.

clarifications.q: Are any of the additions required for launch?
clarifications.a: One might be: the requester says merchants will be confused without it. Nobody has checked.

clarifications.q: Has the team raised the overtime?
clarifications.a: Not formally. Two engineers mentioned being tired in a retrospective.

clarifications.q: Can the launch be partial?
clarifications.a: Possibly. A smaller first release followed by a second one is technically feasible.

hints: Make the growth visible: a list of every addition with its source, size and the reason it is needed, against the original scope.
Present the sponsors with the choice in their terms: the same date with less scope, the full scope with a later date, or more risk; never silently absorb it.
Protect the team by fixing the process, not by heroics: an intake rule for new requests with a named decision maker.
followups: How do you estimate how much the scope grew, when most additions arrived as small requests?
The sponsors want the full scope and the same date. What do you say?
Which of the additions would you defer, and how do you tell the people who asked for them?
How do you handle the evening work, both now and so it does not become the norm?
In your real example, what would you do earlier next time?

rules.ask: The sponsors say a few weeks of extra hours are normal before a launch. What do you say, and what do you do for the team?
Merchants were told the full feature arrives on the date. What do they get, and who tells them?
Your estimate for the additions is challenged as padded. How do you defend it?
The request comes from the team supporting the largest merchants, with revenue at stake. Do you still push back? How?
What did you personally put in front of the sponsors, and what did you recommend?

templates.title: Expanding a product built for one country into several with different rules
templates.subtopic: internationalisation, configurable rules, sequencing, local partners

rule: prices that must include tax in some countries and exclude it in others
a requirement that subscriptions can be cancelled online in as few steps as they were started
refunds that must go back to the original payment method within a fixed number of days

sections.scenario: In this scenario, {{product}} was built for one country. It assumes one currency, one tax treatment, one language, one time zone per city and one set of consumer rules. The business plans to launch it in {{countries}} more countries over {{months}} months. Each has different rules (this exercise's rules; check current docs), for example {{rule}}. The original code has the home country's rules spread through many services, reports and data models. Each country's launch team wants its own changes quickly, and the team that built the product worries that country-specific branches will make it impossible to change.
sections.problem: How would you lead the technical side of the expansion? Cover how you find every place the home country is assumed, how you decide what becomes configuration, what becomes per-country logic and what stays the same everywhere, how you sequence the countries, how you work with legal, finance and local teams on the rules without becoming the bottleneck, how data and reporting change (currencies, minor units, local days), and how you know a country is ready to launch. Then tell me about a real time you took a system into a new market, region or very different customer segment, with what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: The home country must not regress. Rules come from legal and finance teams, not from engineers. The first new country launches in a third of the time available.
sections.assumptions: The situation, countries and rules are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Inventories home-country assumptions systematically (code, data models, pipelines, reports) and ranks them by risk; designs rule types with per-country parameters, owned and approved by legal and finance, versioned and tested per country, with code only for genuinely different rules; fixes data foundations first (amounts as integer minor units with a currency, local days per store's time zone, translations); sequences countries for learning and risk, with the home country protected by regression tests; involves country teams through clear contribution paths rather than forks; defines launch readiness per country (rules verified, reports reconciled, support ready); real example with personal contribution and outcome, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Are the rules known for every country now?
clarifications.a: For the first two. The rest will be confirmed one to three months before each launch.

clarifications.q: Can countries launch with fewer features?
clarifications.a: Yes, if the missing features are hidden cleanly.

clarifications.q: Do the country teams have engineers?
clarifications.a: Some do; you decide how they contribute.

clarifications.q: Is there a standard for currencies and amounts today?
clarifications.a: Amounts are stored as decimals in the home currency, with no currency column.

hints: Inventory assumptions first: search the code and the data for the home currency, tax, language, time zone and rules, and list them by risk.
Prefer a small set of rule types with per-country parameters over per-country code paths; reserve code for the few genuinely different rules.
The first country is your test of the abstraction; choose it for what it teaches, not only for its size.
followups: How do you find every place the home country is assumed, including in reports and data pipelines?
Which rules would you make configurable, and which would you leave as code? Give an example of each from this product.
A country's rules arrive two weeks before launch and one cannot be met by configuration. What do you do?
How do you change amounts stored as decimals with no currency into a form that works for every country, without stopping the home country?
In your real example, which assumption surprised you most, and how did you find it?

rules.ask: Configuration that nobody tests is code that nobody reviews. How do you test every country's configuration before it goes live?
A year later you have {{countries}} variants of one service. How do you prevent them from drifting apart?
How do you store and report amounts across currencies with different minor units, and when do you convert?
Legal gives you a rule as a paragraph of text. Who turns it into a configuration, and who checks it was done correctly?
Which architectural decision was yours, and what did it cost?

templates.title: Project deep dive, re-examined for a local commerce marketplace of merchants, consumers and couriers
templates.subtopic: design decisions, failures, store-local time, merchant isolation, aggregate-only courier data

angle: the data model and the keys
the hardest failure you diagnosed in it
the decision you would most like to undo
how you knew its numbers were right
requirement: menu and price changes visible to consumers within minutes, with the menu as it stood at order time always recoverable
every store report in the store's local day, including stores open past midnight
courier data only in aggregate, never ranking or scoring an individual courier
access for each merchant to its own stores' data and nothing else
scale: hundreds of thousands of stores, each with its own menu and hours
tens of millions of orders a day across several countries
hundreds of millions of item listings updated many times a day

sections.scenario: In this part of the loop you describe a data system you designed or substantially changed, one that other teams or customers depended on. The interviewer will go deep on {{angle}}, then ask how the system would have to change for a local commerce marketplace of merchants, consumers and couriers at a scale of {{scale}}, with {{requirement}}.
sections.problem: Give a five-minute overview: the problem, the users, the scale in numbers, the architecture and your role. Then go deep on {{angle}}. Then reason through what changes at a scale of {{scale}}, with {{requirement}}. If you have never owned such a system, say so, pick the closest thing you have worked on, and be clear about which parts you are reasoning through rather than recalling.
sections.constraints: Your own project only. Describe it without revealing anything a previous employer would not want shared; round numbers are fine if you say so.
sections.assumptions: The marketplace setting is hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Clear problem framing with real numbers; depth on the chosen angle down to keys, schemas and failure modes; decisions explained with alternatives and evidence; honest account of what broke and what changed; a credible re-examination that names the assumptions that would not survive the scale and addresses {{requirement}} incrementally (for example versioned menus with the menu version stored on each order line and change events into consumer-facing views; the store's time zone recorded on the store and the local day computed at ingestion; courier identifiers excluded from analytic tables with minimum group sizes and no per-courier outputs; one access rule keyed by merchant and store assignments applied to every query and export); own contribution clearly separated from the team's, or an honest statement of reasoning rather than recall.

clarifications.q: Does it have to be a marketplace or delivery system?
clarifications.a: No. Any system that moved, stored or computed data others depended on; the re-examination is where we bring it into this domain.

clarifications.q: Can it be a team project?
clarifications.a: Yes, but separate what you did from what the team did.

clarifications.q: How deep should I go?
clarifications.a: Down to keys, schemas, failure modes and numbers.

hints: Lead with the problem and the numbers before the architecture.
Have one decision you would defend again and one you would change.
For the re-examination, start from one record, such as an order line: where it is created, which store, menu version and local day it belongs to, and which of its fields the requirement constrains.
followups: What was the main alternative to your key design decision, and what evidence chose between them?
What broke in production, how did you find out, and what did you change?
Which parts of your design would not survive a scale of {{scale}}? What breaks first?
How would you provide {{requirement}} without a rewrite?
What would you build differently today, and why?

rules.ask: Which parts did you personally design or write?
Is that per day or in total, and what was the peak relative to the average?
A store open until 02:00 local time takes its last order at 01:50. Which day does it belong to in your design, and on the night clocks change?
An order from last month needs the menu price it was placed at. Can your design still answer that after the menu changed?
Which tables or views in your design could identify an individual courier, and how do you keep courier data aggregate-only?
